title: Scaling Quantum Optimization to the Thousand-Qubit Scale with Distributed Quantum Sampling
summary: The Minimum Birkhoff Decomposition (MBD) seeks a sparse weighted sum of matchings and is a challenging optimization problem with applications in network scheduling and energy trading. We scale a quantum-assisted decomposition method by combining single-layer QAOA sampling with Extended Fully-Corrective Frank-Wolfe (E-FCFW) optimization, spectral graph partitioning, and greedy feasibility repair. We demonstrate the pipeline on the 1,354-node PEGASE bus test case (representing a 1,354-bus transmission grid with 1,710 transmission lines), whose 1,710 edges define a native 1,710-variable matching optimization problem requiring 1,710 qubits in the unpartitioned encoding. Partitioning enables distributed execution on IBM superconducting quantum processors. The best reported hardware result uses a 50-qubit partition bound, while reducing partitions to 20 qubits degrades convergence in the partition-size comparison. Larger partitions are more demanding for matrix product state (MPS) simulation, and bond-dimension tests show that truncating quantum correlations reduces candidate quality. The results therefore motivate retaining a substantive quantum sampling task within each partition as the overall problem scales. On the PEGASE-1354 benchmark, repaired QAOA samples achieve lower residual decomposition error than both simulated annealing and uniform random sampling baselines, while spatial circuit packing reduces hardware execution time by approximately a factor of three. These results demonstrate that combining spectral partitioning, spatial circuit packing, and classical feasibility repair provides an executable path for deploying gate-based quantum sampling on thousand-variable constrained optimization problems on current hardware.

AI.tldr: This work scales a quantum-assisted Minimum Birkhoff Decomposition solver to a 1,354-node grid problem by combining single-layer QAOA sampling with E-FCFW optimization, spectral graph partitioning, and greedy feasibility repair, achieving lower residual error than classical baselines.
AI.motivation: MBD is a hard optimization problem (sparse weighted sum of matchings) with applications in network scheduling and energy trading. Direct unpartitioned encoding of the PEGASE-1354 case requires 1,710 qubits, which is infeasible on current quantum hardware, so a scalable decomposition and partitioning approach is needed.
AI.method: The pipeline combines single-layer QAOA sampling with Extended Fully-Corrective Frank-Wolfe (E-FCFW) optimization, spectral graph partitioning to split the 1,710-variable problem into hardware-executable partitions, spatial circuit packing to reduce execution time, and greedy feasibility repair of QAOA samples. Distributed execution is performed on IBM superconducting quantum processors, with MPS simulation used for larger partitions.
AI.result: On the PEGASE-1354 benchmark, the best hardware result uses a 50-qubit partition bound, while 20-qubit partitions degrade convergence. Larger partitions are more demanding for MPS simulation, and bond-dimension truncation reduces candidate quality. Repaired QAOA samples achieve lower residual decomposition error than both simulated annealing and uniform random sampling, and spatial circuit packing cuts hardware execution time by roughly a factor of three.
AI.conclusion: Combining spectral partitioning, spatial circuit packing, and classical feasibility repair provides an executable path for deploying gate-based quantum sampling on thousand-variable constrained optimization problems on current hardware, motivating retention of a substantive quantum sampling task within each partition as problem scale grows.

title: Coherence-assisted quantum state preparation and thermal control through repeated interactions
summary: We investigate the relaxation dynamics and steady state of a qubit interacting with a coherent environment through an energy-conserving flip-flop interaction within the Markovian repeated-interaction framework. We derive an exact analytical solution for the evolving and stationary state, nonperturbative in the environmental coherence. We show that environmental coherence provides a resource for dissipative state preparation by expanding the set of accessible steady states. In particular, coherent ancillas can increase the system ground- state population beyond that of the bath, corresponding to an effective temperature below the bath temperature, and enhance its steady-state purity, with these effects controlled by the interplay between the system energy scale and the system-ancilla coupling. Nevertheless, we prove that the purity of the system can never exceed the purity of the ancilla. We further analyze the thermodynamics of the protocol and show that environmental coherence can modify and even reverse the natural direction of heat transfer, giving rise to anomalous heat flow. Remarkably, for fixed interaction parameters, the direction of the coherence-induced heat transfer is governed by the relative phase between the system and ancilla coherence, whereas their magnitudes determine the amount of heat exchanged. Our results establish environmental coherence as a resource for controlling steady-state preparation and energy transfer in repeated-interaction dynamics.

AI.tldr: Environmental coherence acts as a resource that expands accessible steady states, can lower effective temperature and boost purity (bounded by ancilla purity), and can reverse heat flow in repeated-interaction qubit dynamics.
AI.motivation: To understand how a coherent (rather than thermal) environment governs the relaxation dynamics and steady state of a qubit, and whether environmental coherence can be exploited as a resource for dissipative state preparation and thermodynamic control.
AI.method: A qubit interacting with a coherent environment via an energy-conserving flip-flop interaction is studied in the Markovian repeated-interaction framework. An exact analytical solution, nonperturbative in the environmental coherence, is derived for the evolving and stationary states.
AI.result: Environmental coherence expands the set of reachable steady states, enabling ground-state populations beyond the bath value (effective temperature below bath temperature) and enhanced steady-state purity, controlled by the ratio of system energy scale to system-ancilla coupling. The system purity is proven never to exceed the ancilla purity. Thermodynamically, coherence modifies and can reverse heat transfer, producing anomalous heat flow; direction depends on the relative phase between system and ancilla coherence, while magnitudes set the heat exchanged.
AI.conclusion: Environmental coherence is established as a resource for controlling steady-state preparation and energy transfer in repeated-interaction dynamics.

title: Susceptibility of qudit-qudit entanglement to quantum noise: insights from the negativity rank
summary: One aspect of complexity for quantum many-body systems resides in their ability to exhibit entanglement, uniquely quantum correlations central to quantum computation. To quantitatively explore the diminishing effect that quantum noise has on entanglement resources, we focus on the negativity witness, an entanglement measure based on local time reversal transformations that provides a perfect witness in simple physical contexts. Beyond calculation of the negativity, we analyze the associated eigenvalue spectra of partially transposed density matrices for qudit-qudit bipartitions, finding that higher negativity rank provides greater(reduced) robustness to targeted(depolarizing) noise. In particular, we extend the maximum number of separable states that can be arbitrarily mixed into an entangled pure ensemble while retaining negativity to be exactly equal to the original negativity rank. Furthermore, we report how understanding the role of the negativity rank with respect to the completely depolarizing channel allows direct calculation of (1) certain noise boundaries for the Absolutely Positive Partial Transpose (APPT) subspace beyond which no unitary operator is capable of generating negativity and (2) the maximum qutrit-qutrit APPT purity. Beyond proving tight bounds and contributing to the ongoing search for APPT entanglement, these results expand our understanding of the nuanced relationship between computation with entanglement and practical environments for operating quantum devices.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how quantum noise degrades entanglement by analyzing negativity and the eigenvalue spectra of partially transposed density matrices, linking negativity rank to noise robustness and deriving bounds for the APPT subspace and maximum qutrit-qutrit APPT purity.
AI.motivation: Entanglement is a uniquely quantum resource central to quantum computation, and quantum noise diminishes it. A quantitative understanding of how noise affects entanglement resources, using a computable witness like negativity, is needed to characterize robust quantum devices and to advance the search for APPT entanglement.
AI.method: The authors analyze the negativity witness based on local time-reversal transformations for qudit-qudit bipartitions, examining the eigenvalue spectra of partially transposed density matrices. They relate the negativity rank to robustness under targeted and depolarizing noise, extend the number of separable states that can be mixed into an entangled pure ensemble while retaining negativity, and use the negativity rank to compute noise boundaries for the APPT subspace and the maximum qutrit-qutrit APPT purity.
AI.result: Higher negativity rank yields greater robustness to targeted noise but reduced robustness to depolarizing noise. The maximum number of separable states that can be arbitrarily mixed into an entangled pure ensemble while retaining negativity equals the original negativity rank. The analysis enables direct calculation of certain APPT noise boundaries beyond which no unitary can generate negativity, and of the maximum qutrit-qutrit APPT purity. Tight bounds are proven.
AI.conclusion: The negativity rank offers a practical handle on noise effects, yielding tight bounds and new results on APPT entanglement. These findings clarify the relationship between entanglement-based computation and realistic noisy environments for operating quantum devices.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for Quantum Fidelity Estimation
summary: Quantum fidelity estimation is a fundamental task in quantum information and computing to benchmark the quality of quantum states, and hence of quantum processes, on noisy quantum hardware. Point estimates of fidelity by existing methods generally lack the rigorous uncertainty quantification required for reliable preparation and verification of these tasks. While Bayesian and bootstrap frameworks are widely used for uncertainty quantification, they are sensitive to model misspecification or lack formal coverage guarantees in non-asymptotic regimes. This paper introduces a hybrid "Bayesian-informed" conformal prediction-based framework to provide distribution-free, rigorous prediction intervals for quantum state fidelity estimation which can be used, with care, to approximate confidence intervals with respect to the quantum randomness of Born's rule. The framework requires a point estimator, and we consider both classical point estimators as well as data-driven neural net estimators. We evaluate the robustness of the methodology across a diverse range of experimental challenges, including finite-sample noise, tomographic incompleteness, physical model error, and out-of-distribution data. Our results demonstrate that conformalized estimators maintain statistical validity where traditional methods fail, offering a scalable and reliable approach for the verification of modern quantum systems. The best performing variant of our methodology is based on a class-conditional conformal prediction, as this most closely approximates the conditional coverage desired for a true confidence interval.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid "Bayesian-informed" conformal prediction framework for quantum state fidelity estimation, providing distribution-free prediction intervals with formal guarantees, evaluated across various experimental challenges.
AI.motivation: Point estimates of fidelity lack rigorous uncertainty quantification needed for reliable preparation and verification of quantum states. Existing Bayesian and bootstrap frameworks for uncertainty quantification are sensitive to model misspecification or lack formal coverage guarantees in non-asymptotic regimes.
AI.method: The authors introduce a hybrid "Bayesian-informed" conformal prediction-based framework to provide distribution-free, rigorous prediction intervals for quantum state fidelity estimation. The framework requires a point estimator, and they consider both classical point estimators and data-driven neural net estimators. The best performing variant is based on class-conditional conformal prediction.
AI.result: Conformalized estimators maintain statistical validity where traditional Bayesian and bootstrap methods fail. The methodology is robust across finite-sample noise, tomographic incompleteness, physical model error, and out-of-distribution data. Class-conditional conformal prediction most closely approximates conditional coverage desired for a true confidence interval.
AI.conclusion: The proposed conformalized framework offers a scalable and reliable approach for verification of modern quantum systems. The prediction intervals can be used, with care, to approximate confidence intervals with respect to quantum randomness of Born's rule.

title: Helicity decoupling ultrastrong Rabi splitting from quantum vacuum dressing
summary: Polaritons and quantum vacuum dressing are usually regarded as intertwined consequences of ultrastrong light-matter coupling. Here we show that they can be controlled independently through helicity. We consider cyclotron resonance coupled to a chiral cavity supporting a single circular mode. When the helicity of the cavity field matches the cyclotron motion, energy is exchanged resonantly between light and matter, producing a large Rabi splitting and conventional polaritons, while the ground state remains the bare vacuum. Reversing the magnetic field reverses the cyclotron motion without changing the cavity. The same mode then couples through anomalous processes that create and annihilate light and matter excitations in pairs: the conventional polaritonic anticrossing disappears, while the ground state acquires squeezing and virtual excitations. These two regimes show that spectral hybridization and quantum vacuum dressing are distinct manifestations of ultrastrong coupling, and that a large Rabi splitting alone does not imply a dressed quantum vacuum. Helicity therefore provides a route to controlling polariton formation and quantum correlations as distinct resources in cavity quantum materials.

AI.tldr: Polaritons and quantum vacuum dressing can be controlled independently via helicity in a chiral cavity coupled to cyclotron resonance: matching helicity yields conventional polaritons with a bare vacuum ground state, while reversing it eliminates the anticrossing yet produces a squeezed, virtually-excited vacuum.
AI.motivation: Polaritons and quantum vacuum dressing are conventionally treated as intertwined consequences of ultrastrong light-matter coupling, so disentangling whether spectral hybridization necessarily implies a dressed vacuum is unclear. This work challenges that assumption by seeking a way to separate the two phenomena.
AI.method: The authors analyze cyclotron resonance coupled to a chiral cavity supporting a single circularly polarized mode. By comparing cases where the cavity field helicity matches versus is reversed relative to the cyclotron motion (via magnetic field reversal without changing the cavity), they examine the resulting coupling processes, energy exchange, and ground state properties.
AI.result: When helicity matches the cyclotron motion, resonant energy exchange produces a large Rabi splitting and conventional polaritons, while the ground state remains the bare vacuum. When the magnetic field is reversed, the same mode couples via anomalous processes that create and annihilate light and matter excitations in pairs: the polaritonic anticrossing disappears, but the ground state acquires squeezing and virtual excitations.
AI.conclusion: Spectral hybridization (polaritons) and quantum vacuum dressing are distinct manifestations of ultrastrong coupling, and a large Rabi splitting alone does not imply a dressed quantum vacuum. Helicity thus offers a route to independently control polariton formation and quantum correlations as separate resources in cavity quantum materials.

title: Geometry-optimized hyperbolic codes for modular fault-tolerant quantum architectures
summary: Quantum fault tolerance is a prerequisite to harness the full potential of quantum computers. However, achieving fault tolerance remains a major challenge since it requires optimizing tradeoffs between several intertwined theoretical and experimental parameters, including the encoding rate, code distance, parity-check weights, code planarity, and routing. Surface codes remain strong candidates for fault tolerance due to their simple geometric structure, established decoding methods, locality, and experimental attainability. In this work, we present finite families of hyperbolic surface codes that leverage the optimal efficiency scaling $kd^2/n = C (\log{k})^2$ attainable by surface codes with bounded local geometry. We show that optimizing the periodic identifications can double the code distance and thereby increase the code's efficiency by a factor of four, at fixed qubit count, encoding rate, and parity-check weight. We also address the routing problem of hyperbolic surface codes by introducing a topology-aware algorithm that partitions a hyperbolic code into bounded planar modules while reducing long-range communications demand. Circuit-level Monte Carlo simulations yield finite-size threshold estimates for both modular and monolithic layouts, showing that tripling the long-range gate error probability mildly lowers, but does not eliminate, the estimated error-correction thresholds. Together, these results strengthen the case for hyperbolic surface codes as structured and highly efficient large-scale quantum error correction codes for future fault-tolerant architectures.

AI.tldr: This work constructs finite families of hyperbolic surface codes achieving near-optimal efficiency scaling kd²/n = C(log k)², shows that optimized periodic identifications can double the code distance (quadrupling efficiency at fixed parameters), and introduces a topology-aware routing algorithm that partitions hyperbolic codes into bounded planar modules with reduced long-range communication. Circuit-level Monte Carlo simulations show that tripling long-range gate error probability only mildly reduces—but does not eliminate—error-correction thresholds for both modular and monolithic layouts.
AI.motivation: Quantum fault tolerance is required to fully exploit quantum computers, but it demands balancing several intertwined parameters: encoding rate, code distance, parity-check weights, code planarity, and routing. Surface codes are strong candidates because of their simple geometry, established decoders, locality, and experimental feasibility, yet improving their efficiency and addressing routing in non-planar (hyperbolic) geometries remain open challenges.
AI.method: The authors construct finite families of hyperbolic surface codes that attain the optimal efficiency scaling kd²/n = C(log k)² achievable by surface codes with bounded local geometry. They optimize periodic identifications of the hyperbolic tessellation to increase code distance. To handle routing, they introduce a topology-aware algorithm that partitions a hyperbolic code into bounded planar modules while minimizing long-range communication demand. They then perform circuit-level Monte Carlo simulations to estimate finite-size thresholds for both modular and monolithic layouts under varying long-range gate error probabilities.
AI.result: Optimized periodic identifications double the code distance, increasing efficiency by a factor of four at fixed qubit count, encoding rate, and parity-check weight. Topology-aware partitioning yields bounded planar modules with reduced long-range communication. Circuit-level Monte Carlo simulations produce finite-size threshold estimates: tripling the long-range gate error probability mildly lowers, but does not eliminate, the estimated error-correction thresholds for both modular and monolithic layouts.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolic surface codes offer structured, highly efficient, and routable large-scale quantum error correction, supported by near-optimal efficiency scaling, distance-doubling via periodic identification optimization, and robust thresholds under increased long-range gate errors. These results strengthen the case for their use in future fault-tolerant architectures.

title: A Flash-Based Relativistic Collapse Model for Quantum Fields
summary: Spontaneous collapse models provide a possible, testable solution to the quantum measurement problem, but constructing a relativistic version applicable to quantum field theory remains an important open challenge. Challenges in constructing relativistic collapse models include avoiding superluminal signaling and foliation dependence, controlling energy production, and ensuring vacuum stability. Here, we present a relativistic collapse framework that addresses these problems at the cost of introducing a new space of physical states, whose complete characterization is left open. A modified, history-dependent Aharonov--Albert prescription describes instantaneous nonlocal state updates on arbitrary spacelike foliations while preserving foliation independence. To ensure vacuum stability, we modify the standard unitary evolution through a prescription that we name dynamical vacuum subtraction. The resulting dynamical map is linear and trace-preserving but not positive on the full set of standard density operators. We establish no-signaling by proving microscopic parameter independence, and identify conditions under which standard nonrelativistic collapse dynamics are recovered. Finally, we apply our framework to a free massive scalar field, obtaining finite particle-number and energy-increase rates at leading order in the long-time regime, together with further promising evidence for the consistency of the framework.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a relativistic collapse framework that resolves key obstructions (superluminal signaling, foliation dependence, energy production, vacuum instability) by introducing a new space of physical states, a history-dependent Aharonov–Albert update, and "dynamical vacuum subtraction."
AI.motivation: Spontaneous collapse models offer a testable resolution of the quantum measurement problem, yet no fully satisfactory relativistic extension for quantum field theory exists; prior attempts struggle with superluminal signaling, foliation dependence, runaway energy production, and vacuum instability. The motivation is to construct a relativistic collapse framework that simultaneously tames these four problems.
AI.method: The authors use a history-dependent modified Aharonov–Albert prescription to specify instantaneous nonlocal state updates on arbitrary spacelike foliations while preserving foliation independence; they modify standard unitary evolution via "dynamical vacuum subtraction" to stabilize the vacuum; they employ a dynamical map that is linear and trace-preserving but non-positive on standard density operators; they prove microscopic parameter independence to establish no-signaling and derive conditions recovering nonrelativistic collapse dynamics; they apply the framework to a free massive scalar field.
AI.result: The framework avoids superluminal signaling (via microscopic parameter independence) and foliation dependence, controls energy production, and ensures vacuum stability—at the cost of introducing a new space of physical states whose full characterization is left open. For the free massive scalar field, the authors obtain finite particle-number and energy-increase rates at leading order in the long-time regime, plus further evidence of consistency.
AI.conclusion: A relativistic collapse framework is constructed that addresses the main challenges of relativistic collapse models, yielding finite, physically sensible predictions for a free scalar field and recovering nonrelativistic collapse under suitable conditions. The trade-off is a new, not yet fully characterized space of physical states; its complete characterization and broader applicability remain open problems.

title: Structured leakage in OAM-encoded qubits revealed by distributed quantum feature extraction
summary: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) modes have emerged as an important platform for high-dimensional quantum communication but remain vulnerable to environmental noise and channel imperfections. Here we introduce a logical-qubit representation of OAM propagation in which modes evolve as qubits through noisy quantum channels. In this representation, turbulence manifests as leakage from the logical OAM subspace into turbulence-induced leakage components, providing a unified description of degradation in both single-photon and coherent-beam regimes. We show that turbulence-induced leakage exhibits systematic dependence on turbulence strength and OAM order, revealing structured signatures of information redistribution beyond the logical subspace. Leveraging this insight, we develop a distributed quantum feature-extraction scheme that encodes high-dimensional OAM states into quantum representations and employs quantum convolutional operations to extract turbulence-robust features. Simulations and experimental measurements demonstrate robust extraction of these features across a broad range of turbulence strengths, OAM orders, and propagation conditions. Our results establish a direct link between OAM-channel dynamics, structured leakage, and quantum learning, providing a physics-informed framework for characterizing turbulence-degraded high-dimensional optical states and extracting robust signatures of turbulence-induced information redistribution.

AI.tldr: The paper maps OAM propagation through noisy channels onto a logical-qubit representation where turbulence appears as leakage out of the logical OAM subspace, then exploits the structured leakage to build a distributed quantum feature-extraction scheme that robustly extracts turbulence signatures.
AI.motivation: OAM modes are a key platform for high-dimensional quantum communication but are highly susceptible to environmental noise and channel imperfections, particularly atmospheric turbulence. A unified, physics-informed description of how turbulence degrades both single-photon and coherent-beam OAM states is lacking, and existing characterization approaches do not directly connect channel dynamics to robust learnable features.
AI.method: The authors introduce a logical-qubit representation of OAM propagation, treating modes as qubits evolving through noisy quantum channels so that turbulence manifests as leakage from the logical OAM subspace into turbulence-induced leakage components. They analyze the dependence of this leakage on turbulence strength and OAM order, and build a distributed quantum feature-extraction scheme that encodes high-dimensional OAM states into quantum representations and applies quantum convolutional operations to extract turbulence-robust features.
AI.result: Turbulence-induced leakage shows systematic dependence on turbulence strength and OAM order, revealing structured signatures of information redistribution beyond the logical subspace. Simulations and experimental measurements confirm robust feature extraction across a broad range of turbulence strengths, OAM orders, and propagation conditions.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a direct link between OAM-channel dynamics, structured leakage, and quantum learning, providing a physics-informed framework for characterizing turbulence-degraded high-dimensional optical states and extracting robust signatures of turbulence-induced information redistribution.

title: Fast entanglement generation via cavity-mediated nematic tensor dynamics
summary: Many-body entanglement in atomic ensembles offers the potential for enhanced sensing devices. Entanglement can be generated by interfacing atoms with a cavity. Traditional methods use effective two-level systems isolated from more complex atomic level structures. However, alternative strategies allow entanglement to be generated in atoms confined to a single hyperfine manifold. These strategies enable entanglement in ways fundamentally not available to two-level systems but feature extremely slow dynamics due to requiring strongly off-resonant laser fields. Here, I show that equivalent squeezing dynamics can be achieved much closer to resonance, offering entanglement generation over a hundred times faster than typical experiments. Furthermore, the Hamiltonian can be used to speed up the creation of maximally entangled states via adiabatic passage.

AI.tldr: Squeezing dynamics equivalent to slow off-resonant schemes can be achieved near resonance, yielding entanglement a hundred times faster and enabling faster maximally entangled state creation via adiabatic passage.
AI.motivation: Atomic ensembles interfaced with cavities can generate many-body entanglement for enhanced sensing. Traditional methods use effective two-level systems, while single-hyperfine-manifold schemes offer unique capabilities but suffer from extremely slow dynamics due to strongly off-resonant laser fields.
AI.method: The author theoretically identifies a Hamiltonian that reproduces equivalent squeezing dynamics while operating much closer to resonance, and additionally applies this Hamiltonian to accelerate maximally entangled state generation via adiabatic passage.
AI.result: Entanglement generation over a hundred times faster than typical experiments is achieved, and maximally entangled state creation via adiabatic passage is sped up.
AI.conclusion: Near-resonance operation enables equivalent squeezing with dramatically faster entanglement generation, enhancing the practicality of single-hyperfine-manifold cavity schemes.

title: Demonstration of subspace-search variational quantum eigensolver using photonic orbital angular momentum qudits
summary: Accurate excited state energies are essential for interpreting fluorescence and photochemical processes, yet variational quantum eigensolvers (VQEs) on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware have largely been confined to ground states. Subspace-search VQE (SSVQE) offers a NISQ-friendly route to excited states without ancilla-based overlap measurements, however it has lacked an experimental demonstration since it requires the coherent preparation and manipulation of multiple orthogonal basis states under a shared variational unitary. Here we realize SSVQE on a photonic platform by encoding orthogonal qudit states in the orbital angular momentum of single photons and optimizing a shared variational circuit. We estimate excited state energies for a four-dimensional $\rm{HeH^+}$ molecule and an eight-dimensional Heisenberg chain, thereby demonstrating scalable excited state eigensolving in a high-dimensional Hilbert space. Our results establish photonic qudits as a resource-efficient pathway to excited state quantum simulation.

AI.tldr: First experimental realization of subspace-search VQE (SSVQE) for excited states, using orbital-angular-momentum photonic qudits with a shared variational circuit to estimate excited state energies of HeH+ and a Heisenberg chain.
AI.motivation: Accurate excited state energies are essential for interpreting fluorescence and photochemical processes, but VQEs on NISQ hardware have largely been limited to ground states. SSVQE avoids ancilla-based overlap measurements, yet it had never been experimentally demonstrated because it demands coherent preparation and manipulation of multiple orthogonal basis states under a shared variational unitary.
AI.method: The authors encode orthogonal qudit states in the orbital angular momentum (OAM) of single photons and optimize a single shared variational circuit, implementing SSVQE on a photonic platform.
AI.result: Excited state energies were estimated for a four-dimensional HeH+ molecule and an eight-dimensional Heisenberg chain, demonstrating scalable excited state eigensolving in a high-dimensional Hilbert space.
AI.conclusion: Photonic qudits provide a resource-efficient pathway to excited state quantum simulation, establishing SSVQE as experimentally viable on NISQ-era photonic hardware.

title: Analog quantum simulation of $φ^4$ field theory with a superconducting transmission line
summary: Understanding the dynamics of interacting quantum fields remains a fundamental challenge. We propose a superconducting transmission line for analog quantum simulation of $(1+1)$-dimensional $φ^4$ field theory. The transmission line comprises fluxonium-like circuit elements whose continuous and unbounded phase variables encode a scalar field without Hilbert-space truncation. Their anharmonic potentials provide strong interactions. Tuning the circuit parameters provides access to two distinct regimes. In the first, the transmission line emulates $φ^4$ field theory with a single-well potential. We confirm this correspondence through lattice Monte Carlo calculations of the low-energy spectra of both the circuit and lattice $φ^4$ theory. This regime enables scattering experiments between counter-propagating particle wave packets. The second parameter set yields a double-well potential that emulates $φ^4$ theory in the symmetry-broken phase and hosts degenerate vacua. Interfaces between the two vacua form topological kinks, and the transmission line can simulate kink-antikink collisions. We present state preparation and measurement protocols for both collision experiments, enabling spatially resolved, real-time studies of particle and soliton scattering in an interacting quantum field theory.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a superconducting transmission line, built from fluxonium-like elements with continuous, unbounded phase variables, as an analog quantum simulator of (1+1)-dimensional φ⁴ field theory, and outline protocols for particle and kink scattering experiments.
AI.motivation: Understanding the dynamics of interacting quantum fields remains a fundamental challenge, and existing analog simulators typically suffer from Hilbert-space truncation and weak interactions.
AI.method: A transmission line composed of fluxonium-like circuit elements uses continuous and unbounded phase variables to encode a scalar field without Hilbert-space truncation, with anharmonic potentials supplying strong interactions. Tuning circuit parameters accesses two regimes: a single-well potential emulating standard φ⁴ theory, and a double-well potential emulating the symmetry-broken phase with degenerate vacua and topological kinks. Lattice Monte Carlo calculations of low-energy spectra verify the correspondence between circuit and lattice φ⁴ theory. State preparation and measurement protocols are presented for both collision experiments.
AI.result: The circuit reproduces the low-energy spectra of lattice φ⁴ theory, supports scattering of counter-propagating particle wave packets in the single-well regime, and hosts kink-antikink collisions in the double-well regime.
AI.conclusion: The platform enables spatially resolved, real-time studies of particle and soliton scattering in an interacting quantum field theory.

title: 2 Fast 2 Surgery: Fast surgery on QLDPC codes with $\tilde{O}(n(k + d))$ space overhead
summary: We show that the fast surgery framework of Baspin-Berent-Cohen can be instantiated using at most $\tilde{O}(n(k + d))$ ancilla qubits, improving on the previously achievable $O(n\cdot k \cdot d)$ overhead. This result also establishes that fast surgery can be performed at a cost comparable to the $\tilde{O}(nk)$ overhead required for regular surgery. We build the surgery ancilla by first starting with a dense, but expanding system; and then applying expansion-preserving sparsification methods from gauging and code embeddings.

AI.tldr: Fast surgery can be instantiated with at most Õ(n(k+d)) ancilla qubits, improving the previous O(n·k·d) overhead and matching the cost of regular surgery up to logarithmic factors.
AI.motivation: The fast surgery framework of Baspin-Berent-Cohen previously required O(n·k·d) ancilla qubits, which is significantly more expensive than the Õ(nk) overhead needed for regular surgery. Reducing this ancilla overhead would make fast surgery practical at a cost comparable to regular surgery.
AI.method: Construct the surgery ancilla by first starting from a dense but expanding system, then applying expansion-preserving sparsification methods drawn from gauging and code embeddings.
AI.result: Fast surgery can be instantiated using at most Õ(n(k+d)) ancilla qubits, an improvement over the previously achievable O(n·k·d) overhead.
AI.conclusion: Fast surgery can be performed at a cost comparable to the Õ(nk) overhead required for regular surgery, up to logarithmic factors.

title: Quantum Simulation of a Hyperbolically Driven Quantum System with Superconducting Circuits
summary: Hyperbolic geometry hosts a plethora of exotic quantum phenomena ranging from holographic duality to novel topological phases. However, investigating these effects experimentally remains challenging due to the Euclidean constraints of natural crystalline materials. While recent synthetic lattices have achieved static realizations, they often lack the dynamical tunability required to explore the full geometric landscape. Here, we overcome these limitations by implementing a quantum simulation of hyperbolic geometry within the parameter space of a superconducting quantum circuit. We construct a Hyperbolically Driven Quantum System (HDQS) by mapping the hyperbolic properties onto the dynamically controllable Hamiltonian parameters. By probing the systems' response under geometric quantum driving, we elucidate how the intrinsic geometry of the parameter space dictates observable physical quantities. Furthermore, we extend the theoretical framework to realize ensemble simulation. This generalization enables us to harness the fast coherent control of superconducting qubits to capture essential geometric characteristics, establishing a versatile platform for exploring quantum dynamics on hyperbolic manifolds.

AI.tldr: The paper implements a quantum simulation of hyperbolic geometry using the parameter space of a superconducting circuit, constructing a Hyperbolically Driven Quantum System (HDQS) to probe how parameter-space geometry governs observables, and extending the framework to ensemble simulation.
AI.motivation: Hyperbolic geometry hosts exotic quantum phenomena (holographic duality, novel topological phases), but experimental investigation is impeded by the Euclidean constraints of natural crystalline materials. Existing synthetic lattices achieve only static realizations and lack the dynamical tunability needed to explore the full geometric landscape.
AI.method: The authors perform a quantum simulation of hyperbolic geometry within the parameter space of a superconducting quantum circuit. They map hyperbolic properties onto dynamically controllable Hamiltonian parameters to build a Hyperbolically Driven Quantum System (HDQS), then probe the system's response under geometric quantum driving, and extend the theoretical framework to realize ensemble simulation.
AI.result: The intrinsic geometry of the parameter space is shown to dictate observable physical quantities. The extension to ensemble simulation leverages fast coherent control of superconducting qubits to capture essential geometric characteristics.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a versatile, dynamically tunable platform for exploring quantum dynamics on hyperbolic manifolds, overcoming the static and Euclidean limitations of prior approaches.

title: Attainable Boundaries versus Operational Equivalence: Dual Benchmarks for the Hierarchical Assessment of Quantum Resources
summary: While conventional quantum resource theories quantify utility relative to an idealized set of free states, practical implementations are confined to a specific supply environment---a framework encompassing all states realizable or preparable via current experimental apparatus and design choices, not limited to free states. This work proposes a novel framework for evaluating the relative utility of arbitrary quantum states against the resource set made accessible by these current selections. We specifically focus our investigation on two canonical representations: the set of states reachable via free operations as the attainable boundary imposed by current experimental constraints, and the set defined through numerical optimization as the criterion for operational equivalence. Our framework establishes two core evaluation methodologies. First, we provide a strategy-dependent benchmark by assessing a state's performance relative to the reference set under its individually optimized strategy, thereby quantifying achievable performance. Second, we derive a computable lower bound on this superiority by considering optimal strategies for each state individually, enabling the quantification of strategy-independent relative performance independent of specific experimental setups. Beyond relative efficiency metrics, we demonstrate the practical utility of this approach for resource management scenarios, including the selective extraction of states advantageous for storage and distribution, and the concentration of residual resources. Using quantum entanglement as a paradigmatic example, we prove that distillable entanglement can be fully recovered via extraction and concentration when the reference set is restricted to pure states, thereby demonstrating the practical relevance of our framework.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework to evaluate the relative utility of arbitrary quantum states against the resource set accessible under current experimental constraints, rather than idealized free states, and demonstrates its use for resource management using quantum entanglement.
AI.motivation: Conventional quantum resource theories measure utility relative to an idealized set of free states, but real implementations are limited to a supply environment defined by what current apparatus and design choices can prepare. A framework is needed to assess the relative utility of arbitrary states against this practically accessible resource set.
AI.method: Two canonical reference-set representations are studied: states reachable via free operations (attainable boundary from experimental constraints) and sets defined via numerical optimization (criterion for operational equivalence). Two evaluation methodologies are established: (1) a strategy-dependent benchmark measuring a state's performance relative to the reference set under its individually optimized strategy; (2) a computable lower bound on superiority derived from optimal strategies for each state individually, yielding strategy-independent relative performance.
AI.result: The framework enables resource management tasks, including selective extraction of states advantageous for storage and distribution, and concentration of residual resources. For quantum entanglement, distillable entanglement is proven fully recoverable via extraction and concentration when the reference set is restricted to pure states.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating state utility relative to experimentally accessible resource sets provides a practical, computable, and strategy-independent measure of relative performance, and the entanglement case demonstrates its practical relevance.

title: A lower bound on the overhead of surgery on sparse stabiliser codes
summary: We show that performing lattice surgery on sparse stabiliser codes with sparse ancillas requires $\tildeΩ(k^2)$ ancillary qubits in the worst case. As a result, for codes with large $k$, constant overhead ancillas can only realise a small fraction of possible measurements.

AI.tldr: Lattice surgery on sparse stabiliser codes with sparse ancillas requires Ω̃(k²) ancillary qubits in the worst case; hence constant-overhead ancillas can only realize a small fraction of possible measurements for codes with large k.
AI.motivation: Lattice surgery is a leading approach for fault-tolerant logical measurement and code deformation, and it is often hoped that ancilla overhead can be kept constant. It was unclear whether sparse ancillas suffice to realize the full set of measurements on sparse stabiliser codes.
AI.method: Ancilla-count lower-bound analysis of lattice surgery applied to sparse stabiliser codes, assuming the ancilla systems are themselves sparse.
AI.result: A worst-case lower bound of Ω̃(k²) ancillary qubits is established for performing lattice surgery on sparse stabiliser codes with sparse ancillas.
AI.conclusion: Constant-overhead ancillas cannot support lattice surgery on sparse stabiliser codes with large k in general, as they can only realize a small fraction of possible measurements.

title: Sub-MHz SWAP spectroscopy of two-level systems in superconducting qubits
comment: 12 pages, 8 figures, 1 table. Includes Supplemental Material
summary: An outstanding challenge in superconducting quantum circuits is mitigating loss from two-level system (TLS) defects. SWAP spectroscopy with flux-tunable qubits can detect individual TLSs, but the Rabi chevrons that signal coherent exchange have been observed only for the most strongly coupled defects. Here, we introduce a sequence with fast flux pulses only at state preparation and readout, switched off during the energy-relaxation delay for finer frequency resolution and longer interaction times. We detect Rabi chevrons at swap rates as low as 0.1 MHz, an order of magnitude lower than previously reported. In the dressed-state picture, we fit the coherent swap oscillations to extract the TLS energy-relaxation time. These Rabi chevrons reveal coherent TLSs with a median energy-relaxation time of 10 microseconds, at coupling strengths previously associated with incoherent TLSs. The swap coherence times exceed the qubit T2* limited by flux noise, indicating that the dressed gap protects them from low-frequency 1/f noise.

AI.tldr: A new SWAP spectroscopy sequence using fast flux pulses only at state preparation and readout detects Rabi chevrons for TLS defects at swap rates 10x lower than previously reported, revealing coherent TLSs with ~10 microsecond relaxation times.
AI.motivation: Loss from two-level system (TLS) defects is a major challenge in superconducting quantum circuits. While SWAP spectroscopy with flux-tunable qubits can detect individual TLSs, previously only the most strongly coupled defects showed the Rabi chevrons that signal coherent exchange.
AI.method: The authors introduce a sequence that applies fast flux pulses only during state preparation and readout, turning them off during the energy-relaxation delay. This yields finer frequency resolution and longer interaction times, and they fit the coherent swap oscillations in the dressed-state picture to extract the TLS energy-relaxation time.
AI.result: Rabi chevrons were detected at swap rates as low as 0.1 MHz, an order of magnitude lower than previously reported. The chevrons reveal coherent TLSs with a median energy-relaxation time of 10 microseconds, at coupling strengths formerly associated with incoherent TLSs. Swap coherence times exceed the qubit T2* limited by flux noise.
AI.conclusion: The dressed gap protects the coherent swap oscillations from low-frequency 1/f noise, enabling detection of coherent TLSs at weak coupling that were previously inaccessible.

title: Retromorphic Testing of Quantum Compiler Passes
summary:
Quantum compilers play a critical role in transforming high-level quantum programs into optimized, hardware-compatible circuits. However, verifying the correctness of compiler passes remains challenging, as determining the expected output of large, deeply entangled quantum circuits is computationally intractable. This challenge is further amplified when compiler passes modify already complex circuit structures, making manual validation of transformed circuits impractical.
  In this work, we perform a systematic analysis of unit tests for quantum compiler passes in four quantum programming frameworks (PennyLane, Qiskit, Cirq, and pytket). Our findings indicate validation is dominated by program-content and program-metric assertions, and test circuits are generally small and shallow. Motivated by these observations, we introduce a testing methodology for automated validation of quantum compiler passes based on retromorphic testing and principles from the Hadamard test. This methodology analyzes a compiler pass, test circuit, and expected pass behavior to verify semantic preservation and intended structural modifications.
  We implement our methods in a framework, RetroQ, and apply it to compiler passes in PennyLane and Qiskit. Experimental evaluation reproduced several existing bugs as well as uncovered previously undetected defects, such as flawed symbolic parameter handling, incorrect commutation logic, failure to recognize self-adjointness of gates, and runtime crashes. AI.motivation: Verifying quantum compiler passes is hard: predicting the output of large, deeply entangled circuits is computationally intractable, and manual validation of transformed circuits is impractical, especially when passes restructure already complex circuits.
AI.method: Systematic analysis of unit tests for compiler passes in PennyLane, Qiskit, Cirq, and pytket; then a testing methodology based on retromorphic testing and Hadamard-test principles that takes a pass, test circuit, and expected pass behavior to verify semantic preservation and intended structural modifications. Implemented in the RetroQ framework.

RetroQ applied to PennyLane and Qiskit passes reproduced several existing bugs and uncovered previously undetected defects, including flawed symbolic parameter handling, incorrect commutation logic, failure to recognize gate self-adjointness, and runtime crashes.

title: High-Rate Concatenated Quantum Error-Correcting Codes for Qudits
summary: Qudits provide a larger local Hilbert space than qubits and have recently attracted interest as building blocks for efficient fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC). In this work, we extend many-hypercube (MHC) codes, high-rate concatenated quantum codes, from qubits to qudits of prime dimension $q$. We construct the level-2 and level-3 MHC codes with parameters $\left[\!\left[6^2,4^2,2^2\right]\!\right]_q$ and $\left[\!\left[6^3,4^3,2^3\right]\!\right]_q$, respectively, and generalize the level-by-level minimum-distance (LLMD) decoder originally proposed for the qubit MHC codes. In a qudit $X$-error model, we evaluate the code-capacity performance of the qudit MHC codes for dimensions up to $q=13$. We find that the error threshold increases monotonically with the local dimension $q$, reaching $10.0\%$ for $q=13$, nearly double the value of $5.1\%$ for qubits. Furthermore, for sufficiently large local dimensions, we observe a pronounced waterfall regime in which the logical error rate decreases substantially faster than expected from conventional distance-based estimates. To understand the origin of the observed qudit advantage, we analyze the decoding performance in terms of the entropy of the underlying $q$-ary noise channel. This analysis reveals a competition between the increased syndrome information available at larger $q$ and the simultaneous growth of the typical physical error weight at fixed entropy. These results demonstrate that higher-dimensional quantum systems can substantially improve the performance of high-rate concatenated quantum codes and motivate further development of qudit-based FTQC architectures.

AI.conclusion: An entropy analysis of the q-ary noise channel reveals a competition between increased syndrome information at larger q and the growth of typical physical error weight at fixed entropy, explaining the qudit advantage. Higher-dimensional systems can substantially improve high-rate concatenated quantum codes, motivating qudit-based FTQC architectures.

title: Exact polariton-condensate states via nonlinear Stark coupling
summary: We study a hybrid system of coupled cavities, with or without two-level atoms doped inside. By employing a building-block construction facilitated by nonlinear Stark coupling, we identify a manifold of exact many-body eigenstates that remain analytically tractable across arbitrary lattice geometries and atom distributions. We demonstrate that these exact states exhibit a dual physical nature depending on their spectral positioning: when embedded within the chaotic many-body spectrum, they manifest as quantum scars that violate the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis and undergo weak ergodicity breaking; conversely, as ground states within fixed-total-excitation sectors, they exhibit off-diagonal long-range order and form polariton condensates. Furthermore, numerical calculations of local excitation-number fluctuations suggest that negative Stark coupling shifts the Mott-insulator to superfluid transition toward weaker inter-cavity hopping. Our findings provide a versatile framework for engineering both coherent quantum phases and non-thermalizing states in diverse light-matter architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a manifold of exact many-body eigenstates in coupled-cavity systems (with or without two-level atoms) via nonlinear Stark coupling, showing they act either as quantum scars in the chaotic spectrum or as polariton condensates at ground states, and that negative Stark coupling shifts the Mott-insulator-to-superfluid transition.
AI.motivation: To find analytically tractable exact many-body eigenstates in hybrid light-matter lattice systems and understand how a single state can exhibit dual physical behavior depending on its spectral position, thereby bridging non-thermalizing scar physics and coherent quantum phases.
AI.method: A hybrid system of coupled cavities, optionally doped with two-level atoms, is studied. A building-block construction exploiting nonlinear Stark coupling is used to construct a manifold of exact many-body eigenstates that remain solvable for arbitrary lattice geometries and atom distributions. Numerical calculations of local excitation-number fluctuations probe the Mott-insulator to superfluid transition.
