AI.conclusion: The results offer a versatile framework for engineering both coherent quantum phases and non-thermalizing states across diverse light-matter architectures.

title: Q-Capsule: A Localized Capsule-Based Quantum Neural Architecture for Barren Plateau Mitigation
summary: Variational quantum algorithms are often limited by barren plateaus: gradients vanish as circuit size and depth increase, making quantum neural networks difficult to train. We propose Q-Capsule, a localized capsule-based quantum neural architecture that mitigates this problem through register partitioning, local readout, sparse inter-capsule coupling, trainable data re-uploading, and Quantum Fisher Information Matrix (QFIM)-guided adaptive depth growth. By restricting the dominant support of each observable to a small capsule and controlling inter-capsule entanglement, Q-Capsule preserves useful gradient signals while retaining communication between local quantum representations. As the register width increases, Q-Capsule consistently maintains stable gradient variance, whereas globally entangling baselines exhibit exponential suppression with a log-gradient-variance slope near -ln 2 per qubit. Q-Capsule also produces more structured optimization landscapes, higher parameter efficiency, improved robustness to depolarizing noise, and lower measurement requirements. Its adaptive policy achieves 98.1% accuracy on binary classification and 97.7% on four-class classification, while using approximately 73% fewer two-qubit gates than the fixed-deep model on the multiclass task.

AI.tldr: Q-Capsule is a localized capsule-based quantum neural architecture that mitigates barren plateaus via register partitioning, local readout, sparse inter-capsule coupling, trainable data re-uploading, and QFIM-guided adaptive depth growth, maintaining stable gradient variance and high accuracy with fewer two-qubit gates.
AI.motivation: Variational quantum algorithms suffer from barren plateaus, where gradients vanish as circuit size and depth grow, making quantum neural networks hard to train.
AI.method: Q-Capsule uses register partitioning into capsules, local readout confined to small capsules, sparse inter-capsule coupling to control entanglement, trainable data re-uploading, and Quantum Fisher Information Matrix-guided adaptive depth growth.
AI.result: Q-Capsule maintains stable gradient variance as register width increases, while globally entangling baselines show exponential suppression (log-gradient-variance slope near -ln 2 per qubit). It yields more structured optimization landscapes, higher parameter efficiency, better robustness to depolarizing noise, and lower measurement requirements. The adaptive policy reaches 98.1% accuracy on binary and 97.7% on four-class classification, using ~73% fewer two-qubit gates than the fixed-deep model on the multiclass task.
AI.conclusion: Localizing observable support and controlling inter-capsule entanglement preserves useful gradient signals while retaining communication between local quantum representations, offering a trainable and resource-efficient quantum architecture.

title: Gap Sensitivity and Bottleneck Migration in Sparse Constraint-Preserving Quantum Annealing
summary: Constraint-preserving exchange drivers allow many coupling graphs that preserve the same feasible sector, but exhibit different minimum gaps along an annealing path. We derive an exchange-resolved sensitivity of the normalised minimum gap for fixed-cardinality Laplacian drivers sharing a Dicke ground state, and apply it to identify locally favourable modifications of the driver. Numerical experiments indicate this sensitivity reliably predicts beneficial infinitesimal changes, but its reliability decreases when the same direction is extended to a finite edge replacement. The gap landscape tracking reveals one mechanism of this loss of reliability. Improving the active bottleneck can expose a competing minimum, with a more extensive reorganisation of the low-energy subspace. We call this the "repair-and-expose" mechanism and observe it in both dense quadratic and sparse frustrated objective families. This motivates relinearizing the response when competing minima become co-active. In the tested oracle setting, a tied-minimum max-min update is substantially more reliable than continuing the original direction or optimizing only the incoming minimum. Supporting finite-size search and selector tests show that this local information can remain useful beyond the infinitesimal limit, while its practical extraction depends on the driver geometry and identification of the relevant low-energy competitors. These results connect local exchange-resolved gap sensitivity to bottleneck migration and conditional driver redirection.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an exchange-resolved sensitivity of the normalized minimum gap for fixed-cardinality Laplacian exchange drivers sharing a Dicke ground state, uses it to identify locally favorable driver modifications, and identifies a "repair-and-expose" mechanism where improving an active bottleneck exposes a competing minimum, motivating a tied-minimum max-min update that is more reliable in tested oracle settings.
AI.motivation: Constraint-preserving exchange drivers admit many coupling graphs that share the same feasible sector but produce different minimum gaps along an annealing path. Understanding which local modifications of the driver improve the gap is therefore important, since infinitesimal sensitivity information could guide driver design, yet it is unclear how far such local predictions remain valid.
AI.method: The authors derive an exchange-resolved sensitivity of the normalized minimum gap for fixed-cardinality Laplacian drivers that share a Dicke ground state, and use this sensitivity to identify locally favorable modifications of the driver. They track the gap landscape to study how reliability changes when an infinitesimal direction is extended to a finite edge replacement, and compare strategies including continuing the original direction, optimizing only the incoming minimum, and a tied-minimum max-min update in an oracle setting, with supporting finite-size search and selector tests.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show that the exchange-resolved sensitivity reliably predicts beneficial infinitesimal changes, but its reliability decreases when the same direction is extended to a finite edge replacement. Gap landscape tracking reveals the "repair-and-expose" mechanism: improving the active bottleneck can expose a competing minimum with a more extensive reorganization of the low-energy subspace, observed in both dense quadratic and sparse frustrated objective families. A tied-minimum max-min update is substantially more reliable than continuing the original direction or optimizing only the incoming minimum, and local information remains useful beyond the infinitesimal limit, though extraction depends on driver geometry and identifying relevant low-energy competitors.
AI.conclusion: Local exchange-resolved gap sensitivity connects to bottleneck migration and conditional driver redirection. Relinearizing the response is motivated when competing minima become co-active, and the tied-minimum max-min update offers a more reliable practical strategy. The usefulness of local information extends beyond the infinitesimal limit, but its practical extraction depends on driver geometry and identification of the relevant low-energy competitors.

title: Photonic Chips for Universal Quantum Computing: Retrospective and Prospective
summary: Integrated photonic quantum chips have emerged as a promising platform for realizing fault-tolerant photonic quantum computers. Compared with bulk-optics systems, integrated photonics offer compact device footprints, enhanced programmability, and exceptional stability, attributes that are essential for executing large-scale and computationally demanding quantum tasks. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of recent advances in both discrete-variable and continuous-variable universal photonic quantum computation. We survey progress in fault-tolerant architectures and state-of-the-art integrated platforms and highlight the key challenges that must be addressed to scale photonic systems toward full fault tolerance. Finally, we outline future opportunities and research directions aimed at bridging the gap between current proof-of-principle demonstrations and fully scalable quantum microprocessors.

AI.tldr: This review surveys recent advances in integrated photonic quantum chips for both discrete-variable and continuous-variable universal quantum computation, covering fault-tolerant architectures, state-of-the-art platforms, scaling challenges, and future research directions.
AI.motivation: Integrated photonic quantum chips offer compact footprints, enhanced programmability, and exceptional stability compared to bulk-optics systems, making them promising for fault-tolerant photonic quantum computers capable of large-scale, computationally demanding tasks. A comprehensive review is needed to consolidate progress and identify paths toward full fault tolerance.
AI.method: Literature review/survey approach: the authors provide a comprehensive overview of recent advances in discrete-variable and continuous-variable universal photonic quantum computation, surveying fault-tolerant architectures and state-of-the-art integrated platforms.
AI.result: The review identifies key challenges that must be addressed to scale photonic systems toward full fault tolerance and outlines future opportunities and research directions.
AI.conclusion: Bridging the gap between current proof-of-principle demonstrations and fully scalable quantum microprocessors remains the central goal, with the review charting future research directions to achieve it.

title: When Does Interference Help Learning? Kernel Geometry as a Pre-Experimental Test for Photonic Reservoir Computing
summary: Multi-photon interference is the resource most native to photonic quantum machine learning, yet experiments on photonic reservoirs have reported advantages, null results, and train-only effects. These outcomes cannot be compared: each measures task-dependent accuracy on different tasks and platforms. Here we resolve the question task-independently through the kernel geometry of boson-sampling feature maps. Interference redistributes feature variance across roughly twice as many effective dimensions as distinguishable-particle statistics, generating a large geometric separation between the corresponding kernels. The separation grows superlinearly with indistinguishability, is linear in Hong--Ou--Mandel visibility at small visibility for two to four photons, and retains approximately 80% of its magnitude at the source quality of current quantum processors. Under experimental sampling budgets the separation is learnable on adversarially constructed tasks (accuracy advantage +0.22 plus or minus 0.05) and an order of magnitude smaller on natural tasks, gated by kernel--task alignment. The results reconcile the existing experimental record and supply a pre-experimental protocol: kernel geometry establishes that an interference-specific learning resource exists, and task alignment determines whether a given task can access it; both are computable before committing significant hardware resources.

AI.tldr: The paper task-independently resolves contradictory photonic reservoir results by analyzing the kernel geometry of boson-sampling feature maps, showing multi-photon interference creates a large, learnable geometric kernel separation whose usability depends on kernel–task alignment.
AI.motivation: Multi-photon interference is central to photonic quantum machine learning, but photonic reservoir experiments report conflicting outcomes (advantages, null results, train-only effects). These cannot be compared because each measures task-dependent accuracy on different tasks and platforms, so a task-independent characterization is needed.
AI.method: Analyze the kernel geometry of boson-sampling feature maps. Quantify how interference redistributes feature variance across effective dimensions versus distinguishable-particle statistics, and study the scaling of the resulting kernel separation with indistinguishability, Hong–Ou–Mandel visibility, and photon number. Then test learnability of the separation under experimental sampling budgets on adversarially constructed versus natural tasks.
AI.result: Interference redistributes feature variance across roughly twice as many effective dimensions as distinguishable statistics, producing a large geometric separation between the corresponding kernels. The separation grows superlinearly with indistinguishability, is linear in HOM visibility at small visibility for two to four photons, and retains ~80% of its magnitude at current source quality. Under experimental budgets, the separation is learnable on adversarial tasks (accuracy advantage +0.22 ± 0.05), but an order of magnitude smaller on natural tasks, gated by kernel–task alignment.
AI.conclusion: Kernel geometry establishes that an interference-specific learning resource exists, while task alignment determines whether a task can access it. This reconciles the existing experimental record and provides a pre-experimental protocol computable before committing significant hardware resources.

title: Heisenberg Echo Symmetrization for Gate-Insertion Error Mitigation
summary: Gate insertion (GI) quantum error mitigation replaces involutory gates such as CZ and CX with 2j+1 repetitions of the same gates to nominally amplify noise by the same factor. Analytical and experimental results show that this amplification scaling fails for non-commuting gate noise, as typically encountered in realistic devices. Here we introduce Heisenberg-echo symmetrization (HES), which combines standard GI with an echo inspired by the Heisenberg representation to cancel the leading GI error. In our simulations, HES reduces the absolute fidelity error by one to two orders of magnitude compared with GI. Unlike the more accurate Layered-KIK method, HES is compatible with any hardware and requires only circuit-level access. It enables virtual noise scaling across platforms, potentially reducing sampling overhead substantially. Its agnostic noise amplification also provides full resilience to temporal noise drift. For pure initial states, however, high-rank observables can substantially increase the echo variance relative to non-echoed circuits, whereas rank-one observables incur no additional sampling overhead compared with GI or Layered-KIK. HES is therefore particularly suited to rank-one or nearly rank-one observables.

AI.tldr: HES combines gate insertion with a Heisenberg-representation echo to cancel the leading error from non-commuting gate noise, reducing absolute fidelity error by 1–2 orders of magnitude versus standard GI while remaining hardware-agnostic and requiring only circuit-level access.
AI.motivation: Gate insertion (GI) quantum error mitigation assumes noise amplifies linearly with repeated involutory gates (CZ, CX), but this scaling fails for non-commuting gate noise common in realistic devices. A method is needed that corrects this breakdown without relying on platform-specific or pulse-level control.
AI.method: Heisenberg-echo symmetrization (HES): standard GI is combined with an echo inspired by the Heisenberg representation to cancel the leading GI error. Unlike Layered-KIK, HES needs only circuit-level access and is compatible with any hardware.
AI.result: Simulations show HES reduces the absolute fidelity error by one to two orders of magnitude relative to GI. It enables virtual noise scaling across platforms, potentially cutting sampling overhead substantially, and provides full resilience to temporal noise drift. For pure initial states, high-rank observables can greatly increase echo variance relative to non-echoed circuits, while rank-one observables incur no extra sampling overhead versus GI or Layered-KIK.
AI.conclusion: HES is a hardware-agnostic, circuit-level error-mitigation technique that corrects GI's non-commuting-noise scaling failure, offering large accuracy gains, drift resilience, and sample-efficiency benefits. It is best suited to rank-one or nearly rank-one observables.

title: Minimal Scenarios Witnessing Genuine Multipartite Nonlocality Possibilistically
summary: We study a strong form of genuine multipartite nonlocality (GMNL), where an $n$-partite scenario admits a quantum strategy generating outcomes belonging to a restricted set with certainty, whereas every strategy built from nonclassical resources shared among at most $k<n$ parties fails this criterion with positive probability. This generalizes what is referred to as strong contextuality/nonlocality, or pseudotelepathy, beyond ruling out local models. For the simplest five-party Bell scenario of two binary-outcome measurement settings per party, we use the inflation technique to demonstrate that a game with a perfect quantum strategy witnesses a robust separation from models built from bipartite resources under local operations and shared randomness (LOSR), establishing the behavior is LOSR-GMNL. We provide broader context for this result by investigating its simulability with resources shared among three or four parties under different resource models and alternative definitions of GMNL. A central open question is whether $n$-party quantum resources can achieve such a separation from models built from $(n-1)$-party resources, for $n\ge 3$. We make progress here by constructing a family of robustly LOSR-GMNL games with $ε$-optimal quantum strategies experimentally indistinguishable in the limit from true probability-one-winning strategies for any desired level of precision.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a strong form of genuine multipartite nonlocality (GMNL) where an n-partite quantum strategy wins with certainty while any strategy using nonclassical resources shared among at most k<n parties fails with positive probability. For the five-party binary-outcome Bell scenario, inflation techniques prove a robust LOSR-GMNL separation from bipartite resources, and a family of robustly LOSR-GMNL games with ε-optimal quantum strategies is constructed.
AI.motivation: The work generalizes strong contextuality/nonlocality and pseudotelepathy beyond ruling out local models, addressing the central open question of whether n-party quantum resources can achieve separation from models built from (n-1)-party resources for n≥3.
AI.method: The authors use the inflation technique to analyze the simplest five-party Bell scenario with two binary-outcome measurement settings per party, examining simulability with resources shared among three or four parties under different resource models and alternative definitions of GMNL.
AI.result: A game with a perfect quantum strategy is shown to witness a robust separation from models built from bipartite resources under local operations and shared randomness (LOSR), establishing LOSR-GMNL behavior. A family of robustly LOSR-GMNL games with ε-optimal quantum strategies is constructed, experimentally indistinguishable in the limit from true probability-one-winning strategies.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes robust LOSR-GMNL in a five-party scenario and makes progress on the open question by constructing games approaching probability-one-winning strategies, providing broader context through analysis of simulability under various resource models and alternative GMNL definitions.

title: Experimental Measurement-Device-Independent Quantum Key distribution with Flawed State-Preparation over 300 km
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) promises theoretically secure communication. However, it encounters challenges in implementation security and performance due to inevitable device imperfections. Since the proposal of measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD, the critical step toward practical security is to secure QKD with imperfect sources. The source imperfections manifest as state-preparation uncertainty (SPU) in various aspects, e.g., encoding uncertainty, intensity fluctuation, and imperfect vacuum states. Here, we perform an MDI-QKD experiment and achieve both high practical security and superior performance. We address the general form of SPU and guarantee a tight estimation of the secret key rate based on the operator dominance method. We achieve secure key distribution over 303.37 km, which not only represents the farthest distance in experiments involving SPU but also considers the most SPU scenarios. Our experimental results represent a significant step toward promoting practical and secure quantum communication.

AI.tldr: This work implements a measurement-device-independent QKD experiment that handles general source imperfections (state-preparation uncertainty) via the operator dominance method, achieving high practical security and secure key distribution over 303.37 km — the longest distance among SPU-considering experiments.
AI.motivation: QKD promises theoretically secure communication but faces implementation-security and performance challenges from unavoidable device imperfections. After MDI-QKD addressed measurement-side loopholes, securing QKD against imperfect sources became the critical remaining step toward practical security. Source imperfections appear as state-preparation uncertainty across encoding, intensity, and vacuum states, which must be rigorously handled.
AI.method: An MDI-QKD experiment is performed. The general form of state-preparation uncertainty (SPU) is addressed and a tight estimation of the secret key rate is guaranteed using the operator dominance method.
AI.result: Secure key distribution is achieved over 303.37 km, representing both the farthest distance in experiments involving SPU and coverage of the most SPU scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The results represent a significant step toward promoting practical and secure quantum communication by combining high practical security with superior performance.

title: Robust quantum key distribution with imperfections in state preparation and characterization
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) offers an approach for secure communication over quantum channels, based on the principles of quantum mechanics. However, the inevitable imperfections in QKD systems can introduce critical vulnerabilities, posing significant challenges to the deployment of QKD in terms of both practical security and performance. In this work, we present a comprehensive security analysis of QKD in the practical scenarios involving imperfections in modulation spaces. Specifically, our analysis focuses on the imperfections related to encoding, intensity modulation, and their characterization. We provide a unified framework based on the operator dominance method to overcome these issues and achieve a tight estimation of the secret key rate (SKR). The simulation results show that the SKR in practical scenarios, with parameters characterized from commercial QKD systems, closely matches the SKR under ideal conditions. In the finite case, the maximum transmission distance can reach up to 250 km with total pulse number $N=10^{12}$ and the SKR closely approaches the asymptotic limit up to 250 km with $N=10^{14}$. This validates the robustness of our method against imperfections in state preparation and characterization. Furthermore, the feasibility and robustness of method in measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD have also been demonstrated. Our analysis not only promotes advancements in enhancing practical security and performance but also highlights the feasibility of deploying QKD for actual applications.

AI.tldr: This work provides a unified operator-dominance framework to analyze and overcome modulation-space imperfections in QKD, achieving near-ideal secret key rates and up to 250 km transmission even under finite-key and MDI-QKD settings.
AI.motivation: Imperfections in QKD systems, especially in modulation spaces (encoding, intensity modulation, and their characterization), introduce critical vulnerabilities that compromise both practical security and performance, hindering real-world deployment.
AI.method: A comprehensive security analysis of QKD under practical modulation-space imperfections is presented. A unified framework built on the operator dominance method is used to address encoding and intensity-modulation imperfections and their characterization, yielding a tight estimation of the secret key rate (SKR). Simulations use parameters characterized from commercial QKD systems.
AI.result: The SKR in practical scenarios closely matches the ideal-case SKR. In the finite case, the maximum transmission distance reaches 250 km with N=10^12 pulses, and the SKR approaches the asymptotic limit up to 250 km with N=10^14. Feasibility and robustness are also demonstrated in measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD.
AI.conclusion: The method is robust against imperfections in state preparation and characterization, advancing practical security and performance and highlighting the feasibility of deploying QKD in real applications.

title: Deterministic generation of large-scale photonic GHZ states utilizing spin echo in a solid-state quantum light source
summary: Quantum technologies witness rapid contemporary developments transitioning from abstract scientific ideas and fundamental demonstrations, into systems of sufficient quality and scale, enabling real applications. Photonic quantum technologies are playing a pivotal role in these developments, since photons are robust, easily controlled, detect and measured, thus qualify as flying carriers of quantum information and entanglement distributers. The efforts to develop photonic quantum technologies benefit from the maturity of the classical optical technologies. It was shown that even a source of heralded three entangled photons is sufficient for building large scale quantum computers using otherwise classical optical elements. Here, we demonstrate a novel semiconductor quantum dot based device, which deterministically generate at GHz rates, indistinguishable single photons in a robust Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state of more than a dozen photons. The device utilizes novel natural spin echo concept, provided by the opposite precession directions of the negative and positive carriers' spins in the excited and ground levels of the periodically excited dot, respectively. The excitation rate is finely tuned to nullify the phase acquired by both spins' precession. Our record long GHZ state producing device can yet be feasibly improved to provide higher-rate, brighter and more robust deterministic GHZ source, significantly reducing the overhead requirements for photonic quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: A semiconductor quantum dot device deterministically generates indistinguishable single photons in a robust GHZ state of more than a dozen photons at GHz rates, providing a feasible path to low-overhead, deterministic photonic quantum technologies.
AI.motivation: Photonic quantum technologies are transitioning from fundamental demonstrations to real applications, since photons are robust, easily controlled, and act as flying carriers of quantum information and entanglement. Even a heralded source of three entangled photons suffices for large-scale quantum computing with otherwise classical optical elements, but existing sources are probabilistic, limiting scalability and increasing overhead.
AI.method: The authors demonstrate a novel semiconductor quantum dot based device that deterministically generates indistinguishable single photons in a GHZ state. It exploits a natural spin echo concept arising from the opposite precession directions of negative and positive carriers' spins in the excited and ground levels of the periodically excited dot, with the excitation rate finely tuned to nullify the phase acquired by both spins' precession.
AI.result: The device deterministically produces indistinguishable single photons in a robust GHZ state of more than a dozen photons at GHz generation rates, representing a record-long GHZ state from such a source.
AI.conclusion: This record-long GHZ state producing device can be feasibly improved toward a higher-rate, brighter, and more robust deterministic GHZ source, significantly reducing the overhead requirements for photonic quantum technologies.

title: An iterative Bayesian variational quantum eigensolver with the von Mises-Fisher distribution
summary:
We develop an iterative Bayesian variational quantum eigensolver in which the unknown ground state, parametrised as a real unit vector, is inferred through a von Mises--Fisher distribution sequentially updated from
  Hadamard-test measurements on a single ancilla qubit. Building on a companion paper that treated a single success outcome via exact moment matching, we generalise the scheme to condition on $m$ success outcomes for the likelihood function
  per iteration. Since exact moment matching becomes impractical for $m>1$, we exploit the large-concentration regime, in which a first-order expansion of the log-likelihood yields a closed-form von Mises--Fisher
  posterior with $m$ entering only through a multiplicative weight. We prove that the two convergence properties of the single-outcome scheme---non-decreasing overlap and non-decreasing concentration---are
  preserved provided $m$ lies within an explicitly characterised range. Based on the theory, we propose a measurement-based algorithm and illustrate the convergence on randomly generated three- and four-qubit Hamiltonian matrices, on $\mathrm{HeH}^+$, and on $\mathrm{H}_2$.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an iterative Bayesian variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) that represents the unknown ground state as a real unit vector inferred via a von Mises-Fisher distribution, sequentially updated from Hadamard-test measurements on a single ancilla qubit. It generalizes a prior single-success-outcome scheme to conditioning on m success outcomes per iteration, using a large-concentration first-order log-likelihood expansion to obtain a closed-form posterior. Convergence guarantees and numerical demonstrations are provided.
AI.motivation: The companion paper handled only a single success outcome via exact moment matching; extending Bayesian updates to multiple success outcomes (m > 1) requires a tractable posterior, since exact moment matching becomes impractical for m > 1. The motivation is to enable more informative, multi-outcome measurement updates while preserving the convergence properties of the single-outcome scheme.
AI.method: An iterative Bayesian VQE where the ground state is parametrized as a real unit vector and modeled by a von Mises-Fisher distribution. The posterior is sequentially updated from Hadamard-test measurements on one ancilla qubit. For m success outcomes, exact moment matching is replaced by a large-concentration approximation: a first-order expansion of the log-likelihood yields a closed-form von Mises-Fisher posterior with m appearing only as a multiplicative weight. Convergence theorems establish conditions on m for preserved non-decreasing overlap and non-decreasing concentration; a measurement-based algorithm is then proposed.
AI.result: The two convergence properties of the single-outcome scheme—non-decreasing overlap and non-decreasing concentration—are proven to be preserved provided m lies within an explicitly characterized range. The measurement-based algorithm demonstrates convergence on randomly generated three- and four-qubit Hamiltonian matrices, on HeH+, and on H2.
AI.conclusion: The Bayesian variational quantum eigensolver can be generalized to condition on m success outcomes per iteration using a large-concentration variational approximation, retaining convergence guarantees under a characterized range of m and showing effective convergence on small molecular and random Hamiltonian instances.

title: Quantitative Rules for Parallel Calibration and Drift-Resilient Maintenance of Large-Scale Superconducting Quantum Processors
summary: As superconducting quantum processors scale toward hundreds of qubits, manual calibration becomes increasingly costly and difficult to sustain. Here we address two system-level factors governing automated calibration, namely, crosstalk induced by parallel operations and temporal drift of control parameters. On a 66-qubit superconducting processor, cross-entropy benchmarking shows that single-qubit calibration tolerates full-chip concurrency with minimal fidelity loss, whereas CZ calibration requires a minimum coupler-graph distance of four to avoid elevated control errors. Continuous monitoring of representative qubit and coupler parameters further yields quantitative refresh rules that assign refresh priority by error-budget consumption. These results turn two conventionally heuristic choices, the concurrency density of calibration tasks and the refresh priority of each control parameter, into measurable operating rules. Implemented within an automated calibration framework, the rules support a six-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state with a zero-noise-extrapolated fidelity of 89.64%, distance-dependent logical-error suppression in a single-cycle repetition-code benchmark, and a reduction of the mean single-qubit error from 0.023 to 0.011 on a 337-qubit processor, providing an experimentally grounded reference for the automated calibration and maintenance of current and future large-scale superconducting quantum systems.

AI.tldr: This work converts two heuristic choices in superconducting-qubit auto-calibration—scheduling concurrency and parameter-refresh priority—into measurable rules derived from crosstalk and drift measurements on 66- and 337-qubit processors.
AI.motivation: As superconducting quantum processors scale to hundreds of qubits, manual calibration becomes prohibitively costly. Automated calibration must handle two system-level factors: crosstalk from parallel operations and temporal drift of control parameters, which were previously treated heuristically.
AI.method: On a 66-qubit superconducting processor, cross-entropy benchmarking was used to characterize crosstalk under full-chip concurrency for single-qubit vs. CZ calibration, and to identify the minimum coupler-graph distance required for CZ calibration. Continuous monitoring of representative qubit and coupler parameters yielded quantitative refresh rules that prioritize refreshing by error-budget consumption.
AI.result: Single-qubit calibration tolerated full-chip concurrency with minimal fidelity loss, whereas CZ calibration required a coupler-graph distance of at least four to avoid elevated control errors. The derived rules, embedded in an automated calibration framework, enabled a six-qubit GHZ state with 89.64% zero-noise-extrapolated fidelity, distance-dependent logical-error suppression in a single-cycle repetition-code benchmark, and reduced mean single-qubit error from 0.023 to 0.011 on a 337-qubit processor.
AI.conclusion: Concurrency density and refresh priority can be recast as experimentally grounded, measurable operating rules, providing a practical reference for automated calibration and maintenance of current and future large-scale superconducting quantum systems.

title: Topological Superradiant Universality Classes in Cavity-Mediated Spin Chains
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures. Any comments or suggestions are welcome!
summary: Superradiant phase transitions are fundamental phenomena in light-matter coupled systems. Here, we uncover a novel class of superradiant criticality that is topologically distinct from previously known superradiant transitions. Using cavity-mediated cluster-Ising chains as an illustrative example, we numerically demonstrate that the critical line separating the superradiant phase from the cavity topological phase hosts robust symmetry-protected edge degeneracies, a feature absent in conventional superradiant transitions. Remarkably, although its local bulk critical properties are indistinguishable from those of the previously identified topologically trivial superradiant transition, the two criticalities cannot be smoothly connected without breaking the protecting symmetries or passing through a multicritical point. We further show that such topological superradiant criticality is generic, also occurring in cavity-mediated $\mathbb{Z}_{n}^{}$ cluster-qudit chains, as supported by complementary lattice simulations.

AI.motivation: Superradiant phase transitions are fundamental in light-matter coupled systems, but whether a topologically nontrivial class of superradiant criticality exists—distinct from known transitions—remains unexplored.
AI.method: Using cavity-mediated cluster-Ising chains as an illustrative model, the authors numerically analyze the critical line separating the superradiant phase from the cavity topological phase, and extend the study to cavity-mediated Z_n cluster-qudit chains via complementary lattice simulations.
AI.result: The critical line hosts robust symmetry-protected edge degeneracies absent in conventional superradiant transitions. Its local bulk critical properties are indistinguishable from a topologically trivial superradiant transition, yet the two criticalities cannot be smoothly connected without breaking protecting symmetries or passing through a multicritical point. The phenomenon is generic, also appearing in Z_n cluster-qudit chains.
AI.conclusion: A generic, topologically distinct class of superradiant criticality exists, expanding the classification of light-matter critical phenomena beyond conventional bulk-only descriptions.

title: A Power-Liouville Hermite Orbit: Common Spectral Quantization of the Singular Sextic Oscillator and Fractional-Power Potentials
summary: A singular sextic oscillator in the finite-Hermite biconfluent-Heun hierarchy generates an exact four-member power-Liouville Hermite orbit. Power coordinate transformations with the Liouville amplitude map the hierarchy member $N=4$ to four half-line Schrödinger spectral charts while preserving the physical regular-recessive Wronskian zero set under energy-coupling reparametrization. Two charts are the previously studied $x^{2/3}$ and inverse-square-root conditionally integrable potentials; the orbit embeds this known power-dual pair together with the singular sextic and linear-plus-quadratic charts. On the selected physical slice, the degree-five accessory compatibility obstruction vanishes identically, while the transformed Frobenius index reproduces both published fractional-power centrifugal coefficients. The common endpoint condition yields an exact discrete sequence of quartic Sturmian eigencouplings for the sextic oscillator. Independent two-sided shooting confirms representative eigencouplings and node counts. A matched large-action analysis further derives the first matched-endpoint correction within the leading Langer action and improves the Maslov-shifted effective-level approximation. The construction thus connects exact Hermite solvability, energy quantization, coupling quantization, and power duality within a single spectral orbit.

AI.motivation: Known conditionally integrable potentials (the $x^{2/3}$ and inverse-square-root charts) and the singular sextic oscillator are usually treated as unrelated problems. The paper seeks a unifying spectral framework that connects exact Hermite solvability, energy quantization, coupling quantization, and power duality within a single structure.

Power coordinate transformations with the Liouville amplitude map this hierarchy member to four half-line Schrödinger spectral charts, preserving the physical regular-recessive Wronskian zero set under energy-coupling reparametrization. The degree-five accessory compatibility obstruction is evaluated on the physical slice, the transformed Frobenius index is computed and compared with published fractional-power centrifugal coefficients, and a common endpoint condition is imposed to obtain a discrete quartic Sturmian eigencondition. Numerical verification uses independent two-sided shooting, and a matched large-action analysis within the leading Langer action yields the first matched-endpoint correction.

The degree-five accessory compatibility obstruction vanishes identically on the selected physical slice, and the transformed Frobenius index reproduces both published fractional-power centrifugal coefficients. The endpoint condition generates an exact discrete sequence of quartic Sturmian eigencouplings for the sextic oscillator; representative eigencouplings and node counts are confirmed by two-sided shooting. The matched large-action analysis derives the first matched-endpoint correction and improves the Maslov-shifted effective-level approximation.
AI.conclusion: The construction provides a single spectral orbit that unifies exact Hermite solvability, energy quantization, coupling quantization, and power duality, embedding known power-dual potentials as members of a broader hierarchy-derived family.

title: An Efficient Quantum Circuit for Flow Model Execution Using Quantum Neural Networks
summary: Flow models generate trajectories from an initial distribution to a target distribution by solving an ordinary differential equation defined by a velocity field. Flow matching learns this velocity field by modeling the transport dynamics between the two distributions. Wavefunction flow establishes a formal connection between flow models and quantum dynamics by introducing a continuity Hamiltonian, which drives the Schrödinger evolution of quantum states. In this paper, we investigate accurate and efficient quantum simulation of the wavefunction flow, thereby realizing the efficient implementation of flow models on quantum computers. We first leverage a quantum read-only memory (QROM)-based phase kickback framework for the wavefunction flow simulation, generating probability densities that closely match those produced by the corresponding conventional flow model. To address the high circuit-resource cost, we further incorporate a trained quantum neural network (QNN) into the phase kickback framework, replacing QROM for data encoding. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our proposed method implements flow models on quantum computers more efficiently, since it maintains the accuracy of wavefunction flow simulation compared with the QROM-based framework, and significantly reduces the circuit resources.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates accurate and efficient quantum simulation of wavefunction flow to implement flow models on quantum computers, using a QROM-based phase kickback framework and a QNN-enhanced variant that replaces QROM for data encoding.
AI.motivation: Flow models generate trajectories by solving an ODE defined by a velocity field, and flow matching learns this field via transport dynamics; wavefunction flow links flow models to quantum dynamics through a continuity Hamiltonian driving Schrödinger evolution. Efficiently implementing such flow models on quantum computers with acceptable circuit cost remains an open challenge.
AI.method: The authors first employ a QROM-based phase kickback framework to simulate the wavefunction flow, generating probability densities matching the conventional flow model. To reduce high circuit-resource cost, they incorporate a trained quantum neural network (QNN) into the phase kickback framework, replacing QROM for data encoding.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show that the proposed QNN-based method implements flow models on quantum computers more efficiently, maintaining the accuracy of wavefunction flow simulation compared with the QROM-based framework while significantly reducing circuit resources.
AI.conclusion: Integrating a trained QNN into the phase kickback framework enables accurate and resource-efficient quantum simulation of wavefunction flow, providing a practical route to implementing flow models on quantum computers.

title: Quickly extracting fidelity decay rates in random circuit benchmarking experiments
summary: Randomized benchmarking (RB) with structured circuits is experimentally scalable, but gives biased short-depth fidelity estimates because incomplete ensemble mixing introduces transient modes. Waiting for these transients to decay in deeper circuits can push the signal below the noise floor. This is a well-established obstacle, e.g. in linear cross-entropy benchmarking (LinXEB). Here we overcome this obstacle solely through classical post-processing. We introduce a one-parameter family of estimators that interpolate between the standard LinXEB-type post-processing and a new post-processing technique we call the trace filter function. Under practical assumptions, the trace filter function provably suppresses transient modes, exposing an interpretable fidelity decay at short depth, with theoretical guarantees comparable to standard RB, at the cost of an increased variance. We bound the variance, analyze the evaluation complexity of the new estimators, and develop practical post-processing algorithms. Experiments on a Rigetti superconducting processor validate the method for one-dimensional circuits of up to 12 qubits: where the standard estimator requires depth beyond a 40-layer experimental window, the trace filter function yields consistent estimates below 10 layers. Trace-filtered randomized benchmarking therefore extends reliable fidelity characterization to relevant structured circuit ensembles and short-depth regimes that are inaccessible to conventional estimators.

AI.tldr: A new classical post-processing technique, the trace filter function, suppresses transient modes in structured randomized benchmarking, enabling unbiased short-depth fidelity estimation where standard LinXEB-type estimators fail.
AI.motivation: Structured-circuit randomized benchmarking (RB) is experimentally scalable but yields biased short-depth fidelity estimates because incomplete ensemble mixing creates transient modes. Waiting for transients to decay requires deeper circuits, which pushes the signal below the noise floor—a known obstacle in linear cross-entropy benchmarking (LinXEB). A purely classical fix is desirable to avoid added experimental cost.
AI.method: The authors introduce a one-parameter family of estimators interpolating between standard LinXEB-type post-processing and a new technique called the trace filter function. They prove that under practical assumptions the trace filter function suppresses transient modes, exposing an interpretable fidelity decay at short depth. They bound the estimator variance, analyze evaluation complexity, and develop practical post-processing algorithms.
AI.result: On a Rigetti superconducting processor with one-dimensional circuits up to 12 qubits, the standard estimator requires depth beyond the 40-layer experimental window, whereas the trace filter function yields consistent estimates below 10 layers. The method provides theoretical guarantees comparable to standard RB, at the cost of increased variance.
AI.conclusion: Trace-filtered randomized benchmarking extends reliable fidelity characterization to structured circuit ensembles and short-depth regimes inaccessible to conventional estimators, achieved solely through classical post-processing.

title: Remote nonreciprocal magnon magnon entanglement via the Barnett effect with coherent feedback
summary: We propose a scheme for generating and controlling remote nonreciprocal magnon--magnon entanglement in a cavity magnonic system with coherent feedback.The two microwave cavities are driven by independent single-mode squeezed vacuum fields, with a rotating YIG sphere in the left cavity and a stationary one in the right cavity. For a fixed rotation direction, reversing the bias magnetic field applied to the rotating sphere changes the sign of the Barnett shift, leading to nonreciprocal magnon--magnon entanglement. By tuning the cavity detuning and feedback phase, entanglement can be generated for one direction of the bias magnetic field while it vanishes for the opposite direction, yielding complete nonreciprocity. Coherent feedback enhances the entanglement at an appropriate reflectivity, whereas stronger feedback can reduce it. The relative squeezing phase provides additional control, and an appropriate choice of unequal squeezing factors improves the entanglement at fixed total input photon occupation. With the squeezed inputs kept fixed, moderate feedback also increases the critical temperature for magnon entanglement.Our results provide a controllable approach to preparing remote nonreciprocal quantum correlations in cavity magnonic systems.

AI.tldr: A scheme generates and controls remote nonreciprocal magnon–magnon entanglement in a coherent-feedback cavity magnonic system using a rotating YIG sphere, squeezed vacuum inputs, and bias-field reversal to achieve complete nonreciprocity.
AI.motivation: Remote nonreciprocal quantum correlations are desirable for directional quantum information processing, but achieving controllable nonreciprocal magnon–magnon entanglement in cavity magnonic systems remains challenging. This work aims to provide a controllable approach to prepare such remote nonreciprocal entanglement.
AI.method: Two microwave cavities are driven by independent single-mode squeezed vacuum fields, with a rotating YIG sphere in the left cavity and a stationary one in the right cavity. Coherent feedback is introduced, and the Barnett shift sign is reversed by flipping the bias magnetic field for a fixed rotation direction. Entanglement is tuned via cavity detuning, feedback phase, reflectivity, relative squeezing phase, and unequal squeezing factors.
AI.result: Reversing the bias magnetic field changes the sign of the Barnett shift, producing nonreciprocal magnon–magnon entanglement. By tuning cavity detuning and feedback phase, entanglement appears for one bias-field direction and vanishes for the opposite, yielding complete nonreciprocity. Coherent feedback enhances entanglement at an appropriate reflectivity but reduces it when stronger. The relative squeezing phase offers additional control, and unequal squeezing factors improve entanglement at fixed total input photon occupation. Moderate feedback also raises the critical temperature for magnon entanglement under fixed squeezed inputs.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a controllable approach to preparing remote nonreciprocal quantum correlations in cavity magnonic systems, with coherent feedback, squeezing phase, and unequal squeezing factors serving as effective tuning knobs.

title: Spin-outcome correlations and memory-assisted entropic uncertainty in Bhabha scattering with an entangled spectator
summary: We investigate spin-outcome correlations and memory-assisted entropic uncertainty in tree-level Bhabha scattering, where an incident electron $A$ scatters with a positron $B$ initially entangled with a spectator electron $C$. For the fixed-angle post-selected final state, we compare the total memory-assisted uncertainty $U_A$ for three alternative Pauli measurements on $A$ with the entanglement entropy $S(ρ_A)$ across the $A|BC$ partition. We resolve $U_A$ into the separate uncertainties $U_B$ and $U_C$ and evaluate the corresponding outcome-memory mutual-information sums $G_B$ and $G_C$. This separates changes in the randomness of the outcomes on $A$ from changes in their correlations with each memory. In the parameter regions studied, enhanced $A|BC$ entanglement is accompanied by lower $U_A$, most prominently near high-energy backscattering. An analytic treatment of this limit shows that $B$ factorizes from $AC$: $G_B$ vanishes, whereas $G_C$ increases with the initial $B$-$C$ entanglement. An entropic complete complementarity analysis characterizes the accompanying loss of local helicity predictability in $ρ_A$ and changes in the coherence, predictability, and mixedness of the interacting pair $ρ_{AB}$. These results show that initial $B$-$C$ entanglement can lower the total memory-assisted uncertainty in high-energy backscattering by strengthening spin-outcome correlations with the spectator $C$, thereby identifying the distinct roles of the interacting particle and the spectator as quantum memories.

AI.tldr: This paper studies spin-outcome correlations and memory-assisted entropic uncertainty in tree-level Bhabha scattering, where an incident electron scatters off a positron entangled with a spectator electron. It resolves the total uncertainty on the scattered electron into separate outcome-memory mutual-information contributions, showing enhanced entanglement lowers uncertainty, especially near high-energy backscattering where the positron factorizes from the entangled pair.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand how pre-existing entanglement with a spectator particle affects the quantum-information properties (uncertainty, correlations, complementarity) of a scattering process, and to distinguish the roles played by the interacting partner versus the spectator as quantum memories.
AI.method: For the fixed-angle post-selected final state of tree-level Bhabha scattering, the authors compute the total memory-assisted uncertainty U_A for three Pauli measurements on the incident electron A, compare it with the entanglement entropy S(ρ_A) across the A|BC partition, and decompose U_A into U_B and U_C with their corresponding outcome-memory mutual-information sums G_B and G_C. An analytic treatment of the high-energy backscattering limit is performed, supplemented by an entropic complete complementarity analysis of ρ_A and ρ_AB.
AI.result: Enhanced A|BC entanglement is accompanied by lower total memory-assisted uncertainty U_A, most prominently near high-energy backscattering. In this limit, B factorizes from AC: G_B vanishes while G_C increases with the initial B-C entanglement. The complementarity analysis characterizes the loss of local helicity predictability in ρ_A and changes in coherence, predictability, and mixedness of ρ_AB.
AI.conclusion: Initial B-C entanglement can lower the total memory-assisted uncertainty in high-energy backscattering by strengthening spin-outcome correlations with the spectator C, revealing distinct roles of the interacting particle and the spectator as quantum memories.

title: From Solid-State Spin Defects to Fluorescent Proteins: A Perspective on Quantum Optical Sensing Platforms for Biomedical Applications
summary: Quantum optical sensing has evolved from isolated solid state spin defect platforms to increasingly bio-integrated systems designed for biomedical applications. This review presents a perspective on this transition, spanning nitrogen vacancy centers in diamond to emerging fluorescent protein based spin qubits. Advances in diamond fabrication have enabled photonic cavities, nanomechanical resonators, and microstructured devices that enhance spin photon interactions and room temperature sensitivity. Exploration of spin defects in alternative materials further expands the sensing landscape. Parallel progress toward biological compatibility includes chip based architectures for in vitro and in vivo studies, microfluidic integration, and minimally invasive nanodiamond probes capable of intracellular nanothermometry and nanorheometry. Improvements in surface functionalization have enhanced coherence and sensing reliability in complex environments. Collectively, these advances highlight the progress and remaining challenges toward application oriented quantum sensing for the life sciences.

AI.tldr: This review traces quantum optical sensing from solid-state spin defects (NV centers in diamond) toward bio-integrated and fluorescent-protein-based spin qubit platforms for life-science applications.
AI.motivation: Quantum optical sensing is transitioning from isolated solid-state spin defect platforms to increasingly bio-integrated systems for biomedical applications; a perspective on this shift and its remaining challenges is needed.
AI.method: Review/perspective synthesizing advances across: (1) diamond fabrication enabling photonic cavities, nanomechanical resonators, and microstructured devices that enhance spin-photon interactions and room-temperature sensitivity; (2) spin defects in alternative materials; (3) biological compatibility via chip-based architectures for in vitro/in vivo studies, microfluidic integration, and minimally invasive nanodiamond probes for intracellular nanothermometry and nanorheometry; (4) surface functionalization improving coherence and sensing reliability in complex environments.
AI.result: Progress spans enhanced spin-photon coupling and room-temperature sensitivity in engineered diamond devices, expanded defect materials, bio-integrated chip and microfluidic platforms, and nanodiamond probes enabling intracellular nanothermometry and nanorheometry, with surface functionalization improving coherence in complex environments.
AI.conclusion: Collectively, these advances highlight progress and remaining challenges toward application-oriented quantum sensing for the life sciences.

title: Error-Corrected Memory and Logic on a Heavy-Hex Superconducting-Qubit Processor
summary: Large quantum computations require high-fidelity error-corrected memory and fault-tolerant logical operations. To achieve these with superconducting circuits, quantum processors will need many components operating with low error rates. In practice, fabrication of monolithic superconducting devices produces unavoidable heterogeneity in component performance, which the quantum computer must accommodate. We implement strategies to operate a large dynamic compass code on an array of 156 superconducting qubits arranged on a heavy-hexagonal lattice, making use of the entire monolithic quantum processor and redesigning our measurement schedule to exclude underperforming components. We demonstrate improvements of up to $35\%$ in logical error probabilities for a memory experiment by using a noise-informed decoder combined with strategies to exclude the worst-performing qubits and couplers, along with post-selecting on shots with a low probability of leakage errors. In addition to these memory results, we also observe performance gains of up to $56\%$ when these strategies are applied to measurement-based logic, demonstrated by stability experiments. We furthermore demonstrate high-fidelity fault-tolerant logic through lattice surgery. Through pre-selection filtering techniques, we can obtain Bell fidelities above $77\%$, and further logical gap post-selection using exclusive decoding increases these fidelities to above $97\%$. Our experiments demonstrate that high performance can be maintained in key elements of fault-tolerant quantum memory and logic when working on monolithic superconducting quantum processors with underperforming components, by using a suite of noise-informed quantum error correction strategies.

AI.tldr: Operating a dynamic compass code on a 156-qubit superconducting heavy-hexagonal processor, the authors mitigate fabrication heterogeneity via noise-informed decoding, exclusion of the worst qubits/couplers, leakage post-selection, and lattice surgery, achieving up to 35% (memory) and 56% (stability/logic) logical error-probability improvements and Bell fidelities above 97%.
AI.motivation: Large-scale quantum computation demands high-fidelity error-corrected memory and fault-tolerant logical operations. For superconducting circuits, this requires many components with low error rates, yet monolithic fabrication inevitably introduces heterogeneity in component performance. The quantum computer must therefore accommodate and compensate for underperforming components rather than relying on uniformly high device quality.
AI.method: The authors implement a large dynamic compass code on an array of 156 superconducting qubits on a heavy-hexagonal lattice, utilizing the entire monolithic processor. They redesign the measurement schedule to exclude underperforming components, apply a noise-informed decoder, exclude the worst-performing qubits and couplers, post-select on shots with low leakage-error probability, and demonstrate fault-tolerant logic via lattice surgery using pre-selection filtering and logical gap post-selection with exclusive decoding.
AI.result: Relative improvements of up to 35% in logical error probabilities are observed for a memory experiment. Gains of up to 56% are observed for measurement-based logic in stability experiments. Lattice surgery yields Bell fidelities above 77% via pre-selection, increasing to above 97% with logical gap post-selection using exclusive decoding.
AI.conclusion: High performance can be maintained in key elements of fault-tolerant quantum memory and logic on monolithic superconducting quantum processors containing underperforming components, by employing a suite of noise-informed quantum error correction strategies.

title: Parameter-Dependent Noise Resilience in the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
summary: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a variational quantum algorithm used for solving combinatorial optimization problems, which is thought to be a promising application of near-term quantum hardware. However, high rates of noise in these devices can obscure meaningful results. Therefore, it is crucial to understand and suppress the effects of noise on the algorithm's output. Here, we find that the stability of the algorithm in the presence of noise is dependent on its variational parameters. Using a Pauli noise model, we derive an upper bound on the total variation distance between the noisy and noiseless circuit output as a function of these parameters. Results from noisy simulations support this bound and give insight into the best methods to use for parameter generation in the presence of noise. We also introduce new methods of optimization using error penalties and truncated search based on this bound to manufacture error resilience. We extend this analysis to the quantum adiabatic algorithm (QAA) by taking the continuous limit of the QAOA.

AI.tldr: The paper shows QAOA output stability under Pauli noise depends on its variational parameters, derives a total-variation-distance upper bound, validates it via noisy simulation, and uses it to design noise-resilient parameter optimization, extending the analysis to QAA via the continuous limit.
AI.motivation: QAOA is a promising near-term quantum algorithm for combinatorial optimization, but high device noise rates obscure meaningful results, making it crucial to understand and suppress noise effects on the algorithm's output.
AI.method: Using a Pauli noise model, the authors derive an upper bound on the total variation distance between noisy and noiseless QAOA circuit outputs as a function of the variational parameters. They validate this bound with noisy simulations and introduce new optimization methods—error penalties and truncated search—based on the bound. The analysis is extended to the quantum adiabatic algorithm (QAA) by taking the continuous limit of QAOA.
AI.result: The upper bound is supported by noisy simulation results, revealing that QAOA stability under noise depends on its variational parameters and providing insight into the best parameter-generation methods under noise.
AI.conclusion: Noise resilience in QAOA can be engineered through parameter choice, and the bound enables new error-penalty and truncated-search optimization strategies, with the framework generalizing to QAA.

title: Beyond QAOA: A Review of AI and Quantum Computing for Adaptive Combinatorial Optimization
comment: 34 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Review article. Supplementary evidence matrix (coded data for all 119 papers) included as an ancillary file
summary: Near-term quantum approaches to combinatorial optimization are limited by qubit counts, circuit fidelity, sampling cost, and the difficulty of encoding constraints, while machine learning is increasingly used to configure and control quantum optimization workflows. We call such workflows adaptive: decisions conventionally fixed in advance, from formulation and penalties to shot budgets, backends, and whether to invoke a quantum processor at all, are made by learned policies that respond to the instance, the progress of the solve, or the hardware. This review examines three paradigms, AI for quantum optimization, quantum for AI-driven optimization, and AI-quantum co-optimization, and organizes the literature by the decision being learned rather than by application. A structured review of 119 papers, 67 coded in detail, shows that the evidence is considerably stronger for AI-assisted quantum optimization than for the reverse direction: learning already reduces quantum evaluations, improves initialization, supports decomposition and penalty control, and mitigates noise, whereas evidence that quantum computation improves learned optimizers remains largely confined to small-scale simulation. Experimental controls are thin: 25 of 57 studies include no classical baseline, the quantum contribution is fully isolated in 10 of 24 studies where an ablation applies, and the median experiment uses 17 qubits. We introduce an M0-M5 evidence hierarchy, from simulation to matched-resource practical advantage, and find no broadly convincing result at the highest level. We argue that scaling is increasingly a systems problem: the question is not only whether a problem fits on a quantum processor, but how classical and quantum resources should be allocated across the optimization process. The review is aimed at researchers in quantum computing, machine learning, and operations research.

AI.tldr: This review surveys adaptive quantum-optimization workflows where learned policies make decisions traditionally fixed in advance (formulation, penalties, shot budgets, backends, quantum invocation), organizing 119 papers (67 coded in detail) by the decision learned across three paradigms: AI for quantum optimization, quantum for AI-driven optimization, and AI-quantum co-optimization. Evidence is stronger for AI-assisted quantum optimization than the reverse, experimental controls are thin, and no result reaches the top of the proposed M0-M5 evidence hierarchy.
AI.motivation: Near-term quantum approaches to combinatorial optimization are constrained by qubit counts, circuit fidelity, sampling cost, and constraint encoding, while machine learning is increasingly used to configure and control quantum optimization workflows. The field lacks a decision-centric synthesis and a common standard for judging whether reported gains constitute genuine practical advantage.
AI.method: Structured literature review of 119 papers, 67 coded in detail, organizing the literature by the decision being learned rather than by application, across three paradigms: AI for quantum optimization, quantum for AI-driven optimization, and AI-quantum co-optimization. The authors introduce an M0-M5 evidence hierarchy spanning simulation to matched-resource practical advantage, and audit experimental controls (classical baselines, ablations, qubit scale).

Experimental controls are thin: 25 of 57 studies include no classical baseline, quantum contribution is fully isolated in only 10 of 24 studies where an ablation applies, and the median experiment uses 17 qubits. No broadly convincing result is found at the highest evidence level.
AI.conclusion: Scaling is increasingly a systems problem: the question is not only whether a problem fits on a quantum processor, but how classical and quantum resources should be allocated across the optimization process. The review targets researchers in quantum computing, machine learning, and operations research.

title: Extended Results on Absorbing Boundary Conditions as Limits of Complex Potentials
summary: In quantum mechanics, among the proposals for how to compute the probability distribution of detection time and place along a given spatial surface or in a given volume, two leading candidates involve absorbing boundary conditions (ABCs) and complex absorbing potentials (CAPs) for the Schrödinger equation. Here, we extend earlier results on how the two are related. It was previously shown that ABCs arise as a limiting case of CAPs, but for that a (reflecting) Neumann boundary condition was assumed at the end of the region with the CAP. Here, we obtain ABCs in a different limit using a Dirichlet boundary condition at the end of the CAP region, which seems more practically relevant and realizable.

AI.tldr: This work extends the known relationship between absorbing boundary conditions (ABCs) and complex absorbing potentials (CAPs) for the Schrödinger equation, showing that ABCs can arise as a limiting case of CAPs under a Dirichlet boundary condition instead of the previously assumed Neumann boundary condition.
AI.motivation: Computing the probability distribution of detection time and place along a spatial surface or within a volume is a central problem in quantum mechanics. Two leading approaches—absorbing boundary conditions (ABCs) and complex absorbing potentials (CAPs)—are candidates for this task, and understanding how they relate is important for choosing and interpreting the correct formalism.
AI.method: The authors build on earlier results showing that ABCs emerge as a limiting case of CAPs. Whereas the prior derivation assumed a reflecting Neumann boundary condition at the end of the CAP region, this work instead imposes a Dirichlet boundary condition at that boundary and takes a different limit to recover ABCs.
AI.result: ABCs are obtained as a limiting case of CAPs using a Dirichlet boundary condition at the end of the CAP region.
AI.conclusion: The relationship between ABCs and CAPs is more general than previously shown: ABCs arise from CAPs under both Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions, and the Dirichlet-based limit is expected to be more practically relevant and experimentally realizable.

title: From Majorana to Bloch: two ways to generalize the Bloch sphere representation
summary: While the Bloch sphere provides a canonical geometric representation for qubits, its generalization to pure qudit states ($d>2$) is not unique. This representation can be extended following two different approaches: increasing the number of points, as in the Majorana representation, or using a single point but in a space of larger dimension, as in the generalized Bloch representation. In this work, we compare these representations of pure qudit states by finding explicit analytical relations between them. In particular, a general formula of the Bloch vector in terms of the Majorana points of a given state is provided. We also analyze some suitable extensions of these representations in the case of pure permutation-symmetric two- and three-qubit states, deriving the corresponding relation between them. These analytical results allow us to study, from a geometric point of view, quantum correlations of special classes of two-qubit states.

AI.tldr: This work compares the Majorana representation and the generalized Bloch representation of pure qudit states by deriving explicit analytical relations between them, including a general formula for the Bloch vector in terms of Majorana points, and applies these results geometrically to quantum correlations in special two-qubit state classes.
AI.motivation: The Bloch sphere gives a unique geometric picture for qubits, but for pure qudits (d>2) the generalization is not unique: one can increase the number of points (Majorana) or use a single point in higher-dimensional space (generalized Bloch). A unified comparison of these two representations was missing.
AI.method: The authors establish explicit analytical relations between the Majorana and generalized Bloch representations of pure qudit states, deriving a general formula expressing the Bloch vector in terms of the state's Majorana points. They also extend both representations to pure permutation-symmetric two- and three-qubit states and derive the corresponding interrelations.
AI.result: A general formula for the Bloch vector as a function of Majorana points is obtained, and explicit relations between the two representations are derived for pure qudit states and for permutation-symmetric two- and three-qubit states.
AI.conclusion: These analytical relations enable a geometric study of quantum correlations in special classes of two-qubit states, linking the two geometric representations of pure qudit states.

title: Emergent SSH physics and localization in a cavity--atom system beyond the rotating-wave approximation
summary: We investigate a cavity--atom system beyond the rotating-wave approximation and recast its dynamics as an effective tight-binding problem in the excitation-number basis. The same experimentally relevant light--matter platform exhibits two distinct regimes controlled by the photon number. In the large-photon-number regime, the hopping amplitudes become nearly uniform and the effective lattice reduces to a dimerized SSH-type chain subject to a linear energy gradient. The spectrum then organizes into one or two Wannier--Stark ladders, giving rise to controllable Bloch and Bloch--Zener oscillations and quantitatively explaining the observed revival patterns. In the small-photon-number regime, the intrinsic $\sqrt{\bar n+(\cdots)}$ dependence produces a pronounced hopping deformation, namely dimerized couplings that increase along the excitation-number lattice. This deformation reshapes the density of states, enhances collective localization, and generates an energy-resolved spatial bias of the eigenstates. The corresponding real-time dynamics displays direction-dependent anomalous diffusion together with Bloch-like revivals and beat phenomena in selected parameter windows. Our results show that the same cavity--atom platform can realize both emergent ladder spectra and hopping-induced localization in excitation-number space.

AI.motivation: To understand how the same experimentally relevant cavity–atom platform can exhibit qualitatively different dynamical and spectral behaviors, and to connect beyond-RWA light–matter dynamics to controllable lattice phenomena such as Wannier–Stark ladders, Bloch oscillations, and localization.
AI.method: Recasts the cavity–atom Hamiltonian beyond the rotating-wave approximation as an effective tight-binding problem in the excitation-number basis, identifying the photon-number-dependent hopping amplitudes, and analyzes the resulting spectra, density of states, eigenstate spatial bias, and real-time dynamics in two photon-number regimes.

title: Unitary-accessible coherence-erasure distance: Exact qubit solution and a tight qutrit bound
summary: We introduce the unitary-accessible coherence-erasure distance, which measures the minimum unitary-control cost required to transform a quantum state into an incoherent state without changing its spectrum. The target states are restricted to incoherent states on the same unitary orbit, leading to a geometry different from conventional state-space proximity. We establish inequalities relating orbit-restricted quantum transport, Bures geometry, and the unitary-control distance. These quantities coincide for pure states but can differ for mixed states. For qubits, we derive an exact expression and show that, in the nondegenerate case, the coherence-erasure cost depends on the eigenbasis orientation rather than on the eigenvalues. For nondegenerate qutrits, we reduce the problem to an optimization over the monomial unitary group. We derive the tight universal bound $\arccos[(2\sqrt2-1)/4]$ and construct an explicit eigenbasis that attains it. The resulting distance also determines the minimum coherence-erasure time under bounded unitary driving, giving it a direct operational meaning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the unitary-accessible coherence-erasure distance, quantifying the minimum unitary-control cost to turn a quantum state incoherent while preserving its spectrum, and characterizes it geometrically for pure states, qubits, and qutrits.
AI.motivation: Conventional state-space proximity is inadequate for measuring coherence-erasure cost because they ignore the constraint that target states lie on the same unitary orbit, so a geometry better capturing unitary-control cost is needed.
AI.method: They define the unitary-accessible coherence-erasure distance as the minimal unitary-control cost to reach an incoherent state on the same unitary orbit, and relate it to orbit-restricted quantum transport and Bures geometry. For qubits they derive an exact expression, and for nondegenerate qutrits they reduce the problem to optimization over the monomial unitary group, constructing an extremal eigenbasis.
